legal_issues.issue: Whether a Deed of Gift of land at Pannipitiya is chargeable with stamp duty under the Western Province Financial Statute No. 6 of 1990, and on what base the duty is calculated.
Which limb of the definition of 'value' in section 106 applies where the donor acquired the immovable property in January 1978, and what the Assessor must compare under that limb.
What evidence the Assessor may call for, and by what procedure he determines and notifies the value and the duty.

gold_answer_draft.issue: How an Assessor of Revenue of the Western Provincial Council arrives at the value of the Pannipitiya property for stamp duty on the proposed Deed of Gift, where the donor bought the land in January 1978 for Rs.160,000, spent Rs.900,000 building a house on it, and the property is now worth Rs.9,000,000.
gold_answer_draft.rule: Stamp duty is charged on every instrument relating to a transfer of immovable property situated in the Western Province (Western Province Financial Statute No. 6 of 1990 s.37(a)), and 'transfer' is defined in s.106 to include a gift, so a Deed of Gift is chargeable. Section 48(1) provides that where property is conveyed by an instrument the duty is calculated on the value of the property conveyed. 'Value' is neither the consideration nor simply today's market price: under the definition in s.106, where the property gifted is immovable property acquired by the donor after March 31, 1977, value means the lower of (i) the price the property would have fetched, in the opinion of the Assessor, if sold in the open market on the date the donor acquired it, increased by the cost of improvements, alterations and additions made after acquisition and before the date of the deed, and (ii) the price it would have fetched, in the opinion of the Assessor, if sold in the open market on the date of the instrument of gift. Had the donor acquired the property on or before March 31, 1977, the first figure would instead be built on the open-market price on March 31, 1977. To obtain the determination the deed, with a copy, is brought to the Assessor under s.62 with the prescribed fee of Rs.250; the Assessor determines the duty in his opinion chargeable and notifies it in writing, and under s.63 he may require the applicant to produce documents and other evidence proving the facts relevant to chargeability and amount. Under s.78(2) the attesting notary must separately take all reasonable steps to satisfy himself that the value on which duty is paid represents the value of the property conveyed.
gold_answer_draft.application: The gift is of immovable property at Pannipitiya, which lies in the Western Province, so s.37(a) applies and the valuing officer is the Provincial Assessor of Revenue. Mr. Perera acquired the property in January 1978, after March 31, 1977, so paragraph (c) of the definition of 'value' governs and the March 31, 1977 valuation date in paragraph (b) is irrelevant. The Assessor therefore builds two figures. For the first, he forms an opinion of the open-market price of the property as at January 1978; the Rs.160,000 paid on that purchase is evidence of that price, and he may call for the 1978 deed under s.63, though the statutory test is his opinion of the open-market price at that date rather than the price recited in the deed. To that he adds the cost of the improvements made after acquisition and before the deed of gift, which on the facts is the Rs.900,000 spent on constructing the house, supported by plans, bills and receipts he may call for. That gives Rs.160,000 + Rs.900,000 = Rs.1,060,000. For the second, he forms an opinion of the open-market price at the date of the Deed of Gift, which on the facts as stated is Rs.9,000,000. He then takes the lower of the two. Nothing is deducted because the donee is the donor's daughter, and no exemption in s.39 covers a family gift. If the gift were made subject to a reservation in favour of the donor, s.48(3) would require the value to be taken as if no reservation had been made; no reservation appears on these facts.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: The Assessor takes the lower of Rs.1,060,000 (open-market price at acquisition in January 1978, evidenced by the Rs.160,000 purchase price, plus the Rs.900,000 cost of the house built afterwards) and Rs.9,000,000 (open-market price at the date of the deed), and so arrives at a value of Rs.1,060,000 for the purpose of stamp duty on this Deed of Gift. Both amounts remain the Assessor's opinion of the open-market price at each date under s.106, so the figures given in the scenario are evidence of value rather than binding on him, and the amounts actually adopted turn on the evidence produced under s.63.

answer_claims.claim_text: Stamp duty is charged on every instrument relating to a transfer of immovable property situated in the Western Province, at the prescribed rate.
A gift is a transfer for the purposes of the Statute, so a Deed of Gift is an instrument relating to a transfer of immovable property.
Where property is conveyed by an instrument the stamp duty is calculated on the value of the property conveyed, not on the consideration.

For immovable property that is gifted and was acquired by the donor after March 31, 1977, 'value' means the lower of the Assessor's opinion of the open-market price at the date of acquisition increased by the cost of improvements made before the deed, and his opinion of the open-market price at the date of the deed of gift.

On an application under section 62 with a copy of the instrument and a fee of two hundred and fifty rupees, the Assessor determines the duty chargeable in his opinion and notifies the determination in writing, and may require production of documents and other evidence proving the facts relevant to the amount.
The attesting notary must take all reasonable steps to satisfy himself that the value on which the stamp duty is paid represents the value of the property conveyed.

Because the donor acquired the Pannipitiya property in January 1978, that is after March 31, 1977, paragraph (c) of the definition of 'value' applies rather than the March 31, 1977 comparison in paragraph (b).

The first comparison figure is the Assessor's opinion of the open-market price of the property in January 1978, for which the Rs.160,000 purchase price is evidence, increased by the Rs.900,000 cost of constructing the house after acquisition and before the deed, giving Rs.1,060,000.
The second comparison figure is the Assessor's opinion of the open-market price at the date of the Deed of Gift, which on the facts as given is Rs.9,000,000.
Taking the lower of Rs.1,060,000 and Rs.9,000,000, the Assessor arrives at a value of Rs.1,060,000 for the purpose of stamp duty on this Deed of Gift.
The value so arrived at remains the Assessor's opinion of the open-market price at each date, so the figures in the scenario are evidence of value rather than binding on him.

enrichment.original_background: Mr. Alfred Perera purchased a property in Pannipitiya in January 1978 for Rs.160,000/-. He constructed a house on the property spending Rs.900,000/- and now the property is valued at Rs.9,000,000/-. He intends to gift this property to his daughter Himall.

indispensable_provisions.relevant_excerpt: Before any deed or instrument (other than a will or codicil) affecting any interest in land or other immovable property is drawn by him, he shall search or cause to be searched the registers in the land registry to ascertain the state of the title in regard to such land and whether any prior deed affecting any interest in such land has been registered;
indispensable_provisions.why_relevant: Imposes the primary duty that generates the document list: before drawing a deed affecting land the notary must search the land registry registers to ascertain the state of the title and whether any prior deed has been registered. The search is performed against the registered folio, so a certified extract of the folio is the first document to be called for.
indispensable_provisions.temporal_note: Rule (17)(a) itself was not touched by the Notaries (Amendment) Acts No. 47 of 2011, No. 31 of 2022 or No. 6 of 2024; those Acts amended only paragraph (b) and added paragraphs (c) to (e). The text quoted was in force in October 2021.

indispensable_provisions.relevant_excerpt: When a deed transferring any immovable property is executed or acknowledged before a notary, he shall use his best endeavours to obtain the title deed, if any, of such property, and make an endorsement thereon stating the number and date of the deed executed before him and the nature of the transaction and attach his signature thereto,
indispensable_provisions.why_relevant: Requires the notary attesting a transfer to use his best endeavours to obtain the title deed of the property. This is the statutory basis for calling for the vendor's original deeds, the chain of title, and not merely copies.
indispensable_provisions.temporal_note: Rule (33) was not amended by the 2011, 2022 or 2024 amending Acts; in force in October 2021.

indispensable_provisions.formal_title: Registration of Documents Ordinance No. 23 of 1927
indispensable_provisions.relevant_excerpt: An instrument executed or made on or after the 1st day of January, 1864, whether before or after the commencement of this Ordinance shall, unless it is duly registered under this Chapter, or, if the land has come within the operation of the Land Registration Ordinance, 1877f, in the books mentioned in section 26 of that Ordinance, be void as against all parties claiming an adverse interest thereto on valuable consideration by virtue of any subsequent instrument which is duly registered under this Chapter
indispensable_provisions.why_relevant: Explains why the registry folio, and not the vendor's bundle of deeds alone, is decisive: an unregistered instrument is void against a later instrument taken for valuable consideration and duly registered. The purchaser's protection depends on what the folio shows, so a certified folio extract must be called for and read.
indispensable_provisions.temporal_note: Not amended; in force since 1927.

indispensable_provisions.formal_title: Registration of Documents Ordinance No. 23 of 1927
indispensable_provisions.relevant_excerpt: Subject to the prescribed regulations, all duplicates and copies and all books and indexes kept under this Ordinance may be searched and examined by any person claiming to be interested therein or by his attorney-at-law or agent duly authorized thereto in writing, and certified copies of or extracts from any such duplicate, copy, or book may be obtained if required.
indispensable_provisions.why_relevant: Provides the statutory means by which the document is obtained: the registry books, duplicates and indexes may be searched by a person interested or his attorney-at-law, and certified copies of or extracts from them may be obtained. This is the authority for calling for a certified extract of the folio and certified copies of registered instruments.
indispensable_provisions.temporal_note: Not amended; in force since 1927.

indispensable_provisions.formal_title: Tea and Rubber Estates (Control of Fragmentation) Act No. 2 of 1958
indispensable_provisions.relevant_excerpt: The transfer of ownership of a tea or rubber estate on or after the appointed day shall, subject to the provisions of subsections (2) and (3), be null and void unless- (a) a certificate of consent of the Board to such transfer has been previously obtained by the transferor, and (b) such transfer is effected in accordance with the conditions, if any, subject to which such consent has been granted.
indispensable_provisions.why_relevant: A transfer of ownership of a rubber estate is null and void without a previously obtained certificate of consent of the Board. If the property falls within the Act, the Board's certificate of consent is a document that must be called for before the transfer is drawn.
indispensable_provisions.temporal_note: Section 3 has not been amended; in force since 1958.

indispensable_provisions.formal_title: Tea and Rubber Estates (Control of Fragmentation) Act No. 2 of 1958
indispensable_provisions.relevant_excerpt: means a rubber estate of not less than one hundred acres in extent which, under the Rubber Control Act is or is deemed to be an estate registered under that Act
indispensable_provisions.why_relevant: Defines the term on which the consent requirement turns: for the purposes of the Act a rubber estate is one of not less than one hundred acres which is or is deemed to be registered under the Rubber Control Act. The notary must call for proof of extent and of registration status to decide whether a certificate of consent is needed at all.
indispensable_provisions.temporal_note: The definition section was amended by Act No. 20 of 2005, before the matter date. The corpus text of section 25 runs the defined terms together without their headwords; the quoted words are the definition of rubber estate and the verifier should confirm this against the printed Act.
indispensable_provisions.verifier_note: Definition-to-term pairing confirmed: the corpus defined_terms list for 2-1958/s25 runs coconut estate, local authority, partition action, rubber estate, tea estate, the Board, transfer of ownership in the same order as the run-together definitions in the body, so the quoted words are the definition of rubber estate.

indispensable_provisions.formal_title: Land (Restrictions on Alienation) Act No. 38 of 2014
indispensable_provisions.relevant_excerpt: the transfer of title of any land situated in Sri Lanka, shall be prohibited if such transfer is- (a) to a foreigner; or (b) to a company incorporated in Sri Lanka under the Companies Act where any foreign shareholding in such company, either direct or indirect, is fifty per cent or above; or (c) to a foreign company, unless exempted as provided in section 3.
indispensable_provisions.why_relevant: Prohibits the transfer of title of land to a company incorporated in Sri Lanka where direct or indirect foreign shareholding is fifty per cent or above. Because the purchaser is a private limited company, the notary must call for documents establishing the company's shareholding before the transfer can proceed.
indispensable_provisions.temporal_note: Subsection (1) was not altered by the amending Acts No. 3 of 2017 or No. 21 of 2018; in force since 2014.

indispensable_provisions.formal_title: Land (Restrictions on Alienation) Act No. 38 of 2014
indispensable_provisions.relevant_excerpt: Where the title of a land is transferred to a company incorporated in Sri Lanka under the Companies Act, with less than fifty per cent of foreign shareholding, it shall be the duty of the Registrar of Lands to confirm himself whether the foreign shareholding of such company is less than fifty per cent, by requiring the secretary of such company to submit documentary proof to the effect that the foreign shareholding of such company is less than fifty per cent of the total number of shares issued for the time being.
indispensable_provisions.why_relevant: Names the document itself: where the transferee is a Sri Lankan company with less than fifty per cent foreign shareholding, the Registrar of Lands must require the company secretary to submit documentary proof of that fact. The notary must call for the secretary's certificate and the supporting share records in advance, or registration will be refused.
indispensable_provisions.temporal_note: Not amended; in force since 2014.

supporting_provisions.relevant_excerpt: He shall not authenticate or attest any deed or instrument, other than a will or codicil, affecting land or other immovable property, unless the deed or instrument embodies therin or in a Schedule annexed therto an accurate and clear description of the said land or other property affected thereby, showing its boundaries, extent, situation specifying the district, pattu, korale, Divisional Secretary's Division
supporting_provisions.why_relevant: Requires an accurate and clear description of the land showing boundaries, extent and situation, either in the deed or in an annexed schedule. To satisfy this for a twenty-acre estate the notary must call for the survey plan and the schedules of the prior deeds so that the description can be checked against them.
supporting_provisions.temporal_note: The Notaries (Amendment) Act, No. 31 of 2022, s.16(9)(a) substituted only the closing words of paragraph (a), adding condominium wording, after the matter date. The boundaries, extent and situation requirement quoted here pre-dates October 2021, but because the paragraph was substituted in 2022 it is treated as supporting rather than indispensable.
supporting_provisions.verifier_note: Wording is verbatim but the corpus holds only the text of rule (16)(a) as consolidated to 2024 and paragraph (a) was substituted by Act No. 31 of 2022, so the exact October 2021 wording of the quoted requirement cannot be read off this corpus; sound as supporting authority only, as the researcher treated it.

supporting_provisions.formal_title: Registration of Documents Ordinance No. 23 of 1927
supporting_provisions.relevant_excerpt: Every instrument (except a will) presented for registration shall contain embodied therein, or in a schedule annexed thereto, an accurate and clear description of the land affected thereby, its boundaries, extent, and situation specifying the district and the village, pattu, korale, or other division of the district in which the land is situated
supporting_provisions.why_relevant: Every registrable instrument must describe the land by boundaries, extent and situation. The description in the prior registered deeds is the reference point against which the survey plan and the vendor's description of the estate must be compared.
supporting_provisions.temporal_note: Amended by Law No. 50 of 1982, well before the matter date.

supporting_provisions.formal_title: Prevention of Frauds Ordinance No. 7 of 1840
supporting_provisions.relevant_excerpt: shall be in force or avail in law unless - (a) the relevant deed or instrument shall be in writing, signed by every executant or by any person duly authorised by such executant and the witnesses in the presence of a licenced notary public present at the same time and in the presence of one another, and the same shall be attested by such notary;
supporting_provisions.why_relevant: No sale, transfer or mortgage of immovable property is of any force unless made by a writing executed before and attested by a notary. Only notarially executed deeds can be accepted as documents of title, which is why the notary calls for the notarial deeds themselves rather than agreements, receipts or unattested writings.
supporting_provisions.temporal_note: The corpus text is section 2 as substituted by the Prevention of Frauds (Amendment) Acts No. 30 of 2022 and No. 4 of 2024, both later than the matter date. The requirement of notarial execution and attestation for dispositions of land has been in force since 1840, but because the quoted wording post-dates October 2021 this provision is treated as supporting only.
supporting_provisions.verifier_note: The excerpt is verbatim but is the text of section 2 as substituted by Acts No. 30 of 2022 and No. 4 of 2024, so applicable_to_matter_date should read false on the wording even though the requirement of notarial execution itself long pre-dates the matter; correctly confined to a supporting role.

supporting_provisions.formal_title: Tea and Rubber Estates (Control of Fragmentation) Act No. 2 of 1958
supporting_provisions.relevant_excerpt: Where a certificate of consent to the transfer of ownership of a tea or rubber estate is issued by the Board, such certificate shall be attached to the deed by which such transfer is effected, and the notary attesting such deed shall in his attestation state that such certificate has been issued in respect of such transfer and specify the number, if any, and the date of issue of such certificate.
supporting_provisions.why_relevant: Shows the form the requirement takes in practice: the certificate of consent must be attached to the deed and its number and date recited in the attestation. It confirms that the certificate is a document the notary physically calls for and keeps with the deed.
supporting_provisions.temporal_note: Not amended; in force since 1958.

supporting_provisions.formal_title: Land (Restrictions on Alienation) Act No. 38 of 2014
supporting_provisions.subsection: definitions of foreigner and foreign company
supporting_provisions.relevant_excerpt: means a person who is not a citizen of Sri Lanka; means a company or a body of persons incorporated under the laws of any country other than Sri Lanka;
supporting_provisions.why_relevant: Defines foreigner and foreign company, the terms by which the shareholding of the purchaser company is measured.
supporting_provisions.temporal_note: In force since 2014. The corpus text of section 25 runs the defined terms together without their headwords; the verifier should confirm the pairing of definition to term against the printed Act.
supporting_provisions.verifier_note: Pairing confirmed the same way: the defined_terms order for 38-2014/s25 places foreigner and foreign company exactly where the two quoted definitions fall in the body.

supporting_provisions.relevant_excerpt: A company shall keep the following records available for inspection in the manner described in section 121 by any person who serves written notice of such intention to inspect on the company,:- (a) the certificate of incorporation of the company; (b) the articles of the company, if they are not the model articles; (c) the share register; (d) the register of directors and secretaries; (e) particulars of the registered office of the company; (f) copies of the instruments creating or evidencing charges and the register of charges kept under sections 109 and 110.
supporting_provisions.why_relevant: Identifies the corporate records that can be called for and inspected: the certificate of incorporation, the articles, the share register, the register of directors and secretaries and the register of charges. These are the documents from which the purchaser's capacity, its authorised signatories and its shareholding are established.
supporting_provisions.temporal_note: In force since 2007; not affected by the Companies (Amendment) Act, No. 13 of 2019.

supporting_provisions.relevant_excerpt: the maximum extent of agricultural land which may be owned by any person, in this Law referred to as the " ceiling ", shall (a) if such land consists exclusively of paddy land, be twenty-five acres; or (b) if such land does not consist exclusively of paddy land, be fifty acres, so however that the total extent of any paddy land, if any, comprised in such fifty acres shall not exceed the ceiling on paddy land specified in paragraph (a).
supporting_provisions.why_relevant: Fixes the ceiling on agricultural land at fifty acres where the land is not exclusively paddy. The notary must know the total agricultural landholding of the vendor and, after the transfer, of the purchaser's shareholders, so a declaration of agricultural landholdings is called for.
supporting_provisions.temporal_note: Amended by Law No. 39 of 1981, before the matter date.
supporting_provisions.verifier_note: Section 3(2) vests only land held in excess of the ceiling at the commencement of the Law; what makes the ceiling bite on a 2021 acquisition is section 5(1), which the map omitted and which is added as PROV-M052-902.

supporting_provisions.relevant_excerpt: For the purposes of this Law, where any agricultural land is owned by a private company or co-operative society, the shareholders of such company, or society, as the case may be, shall be deemed to own such land for the purposes of section 3, in proportion to the shares held by each shareholder of such company, or society, as the case may be.
supporting_provisions.why_relevant: Where agricultural land is owned by a private company, the shareholders are deemed to own it in proportion to their shares for ceiling purposes. This is why the shareholding of the purchaser company, and not only its corporate identity, has to be documented.
supporting_provisions.temporal_note: Not amended; in force since 1972.

supporting_provisions.relevant_excerpt: No instrument chargeable with stamp duty shall be received or admitted in evidence by any person having by law or consent of parties authority to receive evidence or registered or authenticated or acted upon by any person or by any officer in a public office or corporation or bank or approved credit agency unless such instrument is duly stamped.
supporting_provisions.why_relevant: An instrument chargeable with stamp duty cannot be registered, authenticated or acted upon unless duly stamped. Proof that stamp duty was paid on the deeds in the chain is among the documents called for.
supporting_provisions.temporal_note: Not amended; in force since 1982.
supporting_provisions.verifier_note: Checked against the Stamp Duty (Special Provisions) Act: section 13 of Act No. 12 of 2006 expressly carves out instruments relating to the transfer of immovable property, so section 33 of Act No. 43 of 1982 was still operative for this transaction in October 2021.

supporting_provisions.relevant_excerpt: of lands or immovable property, by a title adverse to or independent of that of the claimant or plaintiff in such action (that is to say, a possession unaccompanied by payment of rent or produce, or performance of service or duty, or by any other act by the possessor, from which an acknowledgment of a right existing in another person would fairly and naturally be inferred) for ten years previous to the bringing of such action, shall entitle the defendant to a decree in his favour with costs.
supporting_provisions.why_relevant: Ten years of undisturbed and uninterrupted adverse possession gives a good title against the paper owner. Documents alone therefore do not settle title: evidence of who has possessed the land, and of any adverse occupation, must also be called for.
supporting_provisions.temporal_note: The Prescription (Amendment) Act, No. 26 of 2014 did not alter the ten-year period in section 3; in force at the matter date.

supporting_provisions.relevant_excerpt: Provided that if the parties to the transaction authorize the notary in writing to dispense with the search, the search shall not be compulsory, but he shall before the deed or instrument is tendered for registration write at the head thereof the reference to the previous registration, if any.
supporting_provisions.why_relevant: Added by the verifier. The search duty in rule (17)(a) on which the whole document list rests is not absolute: the parties may authorise the notary in writing to dispense with the search, in which case the notary must still write the reference to the previous registration at the head of the deed before it is tendered for registration. A statement of the search duty without this proviso overstates the rule.
supporting_provisions.temporal_note: The proviso closes rule (17) in the corpus text of section 31 consolidated to 2024. The corpus amendment_events for section 31 record the 2022 and 2024 changes against the surrounding rules and paragraphs, not against this proviso, which is long-standing and was in force in October 2021.
supporting_provisions.verifier_note: Excerpt checked verbatim against 1-1907/s31; added because the map cited rule (17)(a) without its qualifying proviso.

supporting_provisions.relevant_excerpt: Where after the date of commencement of this Law any person becomes the owner of agricultural land in excess of the ceiling, any such land owned by such person in excess of the ceiling shall as from that date- (a) be deemed to vest in the Commission; and (b) be deemed to be held by that person under a statutory lease from the Commission.
supporting_provisions.why_relevant: Added by the verifier. Section 3(2) vests only the excess held at the commencement of the Law in 1972; section 5(1) is what makes the fifty-acre ceiling operate against a person who becomes an owner afterwards. It is the provision that makes a declaration of the agricultural landholdings of the vendor and of the purchaser shareholders worth calling for in a 2021 purchase; without it the Land Reform Law limb of the answer does not connect to the facts.
supporting_provisions.temporal_note: The corpus records amendments to section 5 by Law No. 39 of 1981 s.3 and Act No. 14 of 1986 s.2, both well before the matter reference date of October 2021; subsection (2), which the quoted text does not rely on, carries the later wording.
supporting_provisions.verifier_note: Excerpt checked verbatim against 1-1972/s5; added to close the gap between the ceiling in section 3 and a post-1972 acquisition.

legal_issues.issue: What documents the notary must obtain in order to discharge the statutory duty to ascertain the state of the title before drawing a deed affecting the land.
Which documents establish the chain of title and the description of a twenty-acre estate, and how registration and stamping affect their value as title documents.

Whether a certificate of consent of the fragmentation Board is among the documents to be called for, which turns on whether a twenty-acre rubber property falls within the statutory definition of a rubber estate.
What documents are required because the purchaser is a private limited company, in particular proof of its incorporation, its authority to purchase and its level of foreign shareholding.
What non-documentary matters, namely possession, encumbrances and agricultural landholdings, must be evidenced alongside the deeds.

gold_answer_draft.issue: What documents an attorney-at-law and notary must call for in order to examine the title of a twenty-acre rubber estate in Kalutara that a Sri Lankan private limited company proposes to buy, and which statutory duties fix that list.
gold_answer_draft.rule: Before drawing any deed affecting an interest in land the notary must search or cause to be searched the registers in the land registry to ascertain the state of the title and whether any prior deed affecting the land has been registered (Notaries Ordinance s.31 rule (17)(a)). The registry books, duplicates and indexes may be searched by a person interested or his attorney-at-law, and certified copies of or extracts from them may be obtained (Registration of Documents Ordinance s.42), so the search is reduced to a certified extract of the relevant folio. That extract governs the purchaser's position because an unregistered instrument is void against a later instrument taken for valuable consideration and duly registered (Registration of Documents Ordinance s.7). The notary must also use his best endeavours to obtain the title deed of the property (Notaries Ordinance s.31 rule (33)), and only notarially executed and attested writings can operate as dispositions of land at all (Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.2). The deed and the registered instruments must describe the land by boundaries, extent and situation (Notaries Ordinance s.31 rule (16)(a); Registration of Documents Ordinance s.13(1)), which requires the survey plan and the schedules of the earlier deeds. An instrument chargeable with stamp duty cannot be registered or acted upon unless duly stamped (Stamp Duty Act s.33). Paper title is not conclusive: ten years of undisturbed adverse possession entitles the possessor to a decree (Prescription Ordinance s.3). Where the property is a rubber estate within the Tea and Rubber Estates (Control of Fragmentation) Act, a transfer of ownership is null and void without a previously obtained certificate of consent of the Board, which must be attached to the deed (s.3(1) and s.3(4)); but a rubber estate for that Act means one of not less than one hundred acres registered under the Rubber Control Act (s.25). Agricultural land above fifty acres is subject to the ceiling (Land Reform Law s.3), and where such land is owned by a private company its shareholders are deemed to own it in proportion to their shares (s.8). Transfer of title of land to a Sri Lankan company with direct or indirect foreign shareholding of fifty per cent or above is prohibited (Land (Restrictions on Alienation) Act s.2(1)(b)), and where the transferee is a Sri Lankan company with less than fifty per cent foreign shareholding the Registrar of Lands must require the company secretary to submit documentary proof of that fact (s.4(3)); the certificate of incorporation, articles, share register, register of directors and secretaries and register of charges are records the company must keep available for inspection (Companies Act s.120).
gold_answer_draft.application: Applying these rules to the estate at Bombuwala, the following must be called for. First, the vendor's chain of notarial deeds, namely Deed of Transfer No. 4562 of 2003, Deed of Gift No. 1120 of 1979 and the earlier deeds behind them, together with any testamentary or partition proceedings through which the land devolved, since only notarially attested writings can pass title (Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.2) and the notary is bound to obtain the title deed (Notaries Ordinance s.31 rule (33)). Second, a certified extract of the folio of the Kalutara Land Registry in which the land is registered, together with certified copies of every instrument noted on it, obtained under s.42 of the Registration of Documents Ordinance in performance of the search duty under s.31 rule (17)(a); this is what discloses Mortgage Bond No. 987 of 2016, and because of s.7 of that Ordinance the purchaser's protection depends on the state of the register rather than on the vendor's assurance. Third, the instrument of discharge or a formal release of Bond No. 987, since the vendor's statement that the loan is settled is not itself a document of title. Fourth, Plan No. 2143 of 1998 and a current survey plan and report, so that the description by boundaries and extent required by s.31 rule (16)(a) and by s.13(1) of the Registration of Documents Ordinance can be checked against the ground; the two acres fenced by the neighbour for fifteen years must be identified on that survey, because under s.3 of the Prescription Ordinance such possession may already have displaced the paper title to that portion, so evidence of possession and of the neighbour's claim must be called for as well. Fifth, proof that stamp duty was duly paid on the deeds in the chain, since s.33 of the Stamp Duty Act denies effect to an instrument that is not duly stamped. Sixth, the extent and registration status of the estate: the property is twenty acres, so it is below the one hundred acres required by s.25 of the Tea and Rubber Estates (Control of Fragmentation) Act, and the certificate of consent contemplated by s.3(1) and s.3(4) of that Act is not called for, but the extent and registration must be documented before that conclusion can be drawn. Seventh, a declaration of the vendor's agricultural landholdings, and of the holdings of the purchaser's shareholders, to test the fifty-acre ceiling in s.3 of the Land Reform Law read with the deeming provision in s.8. Eighth, the purchaser's own corporate documents, namely the certificate of incorporation, articles, share register, register of directors and secretaries and a board resolution authorising the purchase, and, because thirty per cent of its shares are held by a person who is not a citizen of Sri Lanka, a certificate of the company secretary with the share register behind it showing that foreign shareholding is below fifty per cent, which s.4(3) of the Land (Restrictions on Alienation) Act requires the Registrar of Lands to call for and without which registration will be refused.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: The documents to be called for are: the vendor's original chain of notarial title deeds and any testamentary or partition proceedings in the chain; a certified extract of the relevant folio of the Kalutara Land Registry with certified copies of the registered instruments noted on it; the discharge of the registered mortgage bond; the survey plan and a current survey report with evidence of possession, including the position of the neighbour occupying two acres; proof of payment of stamp duty on the deeds in the chain; documents establishing the extent and registration status of the estate, which on these facts show that no certificate of consent of the fragmentation Board is required because the estate is twenty acres and not one hundred; declarations of the agricultural landholdings of the vendor and of the purchaser's shareholders; and the purchaser's certificate of incorporation, articles, share register, register of directors and secretaries, board resolution and a company secretary's certificate of foreign shareholding below fifty per cent. The examination is not complete on the papers alone: possession must be verified on the ground, and the undischarged bond and the encroached two acres must be resolved before the transfer is drawn.

answer_claims.claim_text: Before drawing a deed affecting an interest in land the notary must search the registers in the land registry to ascertain the state of the title and whether any prior deed affecting the land has been registered.
The registry books, duplicates and indexes may be searched by a person interested or his attorney-at-law, and certified copies of or extracts from them may be obtained.
An unregistered instrument is void against a later instrument affecting the same land that was taken for valuable consideration and duly registered.
The notary attesting a transfer of immovable property must use his best endeavours to obtain the title deed of that property.
Only a writing executed before and attested by a notary can operate as a sale, transfer or mortgage of immovable property.
The deed and every registrable instrument must describe the land by its boundaries, extent and situation, in the body or in an annexed schedule.
An instrument chargeable with stamp duty cannot be registered, authenticated or acted upon unless it is duly stamped.
Ten years of undisturbed and uninterrupted possession adverse to the paper owner entitles the possessor to a decree in his favour.

A transfer of ownership of a rubber estate is null and void unless a certificate of consent of the Board has been previously obtained, and that certificate must be attached to the deed and recited in the attestation.
For that Act a rubber estate means an estate of not less than one hundred acres in extent which is or is deemed to be registered under the Rubber Control Act.

The maximum extent of agricultural land that may be owned by any person is fifty acres where the land is not exclusively paddy, and where such land is owned by a private company its shareholders are deemed to own it in proportion to their shares.
Transfer of title of land to a company incorporated in Sri Lanka is prohibited where direct or indirect foreign shareholding in that company is fifty per cent or above.

Where the transferee is a company incorporated in Sri Lanka with less than fifty per cent foreign shareholding, the Registrar of Lands must require the company secretary to submit documentary proof that foreign shareholding is below fifty per cent.
A company must keep its certificate of incorporation, articles, share register, register of directors and secretaries and register of charges available for inspection.

The vendor's chain of notarial deeds, beginning with Deed of Transfer No. 4562 of 2003 and Deed of Gift No. 1120 of 1979, together with any testamentary or partition proceedings behind them, must be called for.

A certified extract of the folio of the Kalutara Land Registry, with certified copies of the instruments noted on it, must be called for; it is what discloses the registered mortgage bond and it governs priority between the purchaser and earlier claimants.
The discharge or release of Mortgage Bond No. 987 of 2016 must be called for, because the vendor's statement that the loan has been settled does not remove the entry from the register.
Plan No. 2143 of 1998 and a current survey plan and report must be called for so that the boundaries and extent stated in the deeds can be checked against the ground.

Evidence of possession must be called for, and the two acres fenced by the neighbour for fifteen years must be identified on the survey, because possession of that length may have displaced the paper title to that portion.
Proof that stamp duty was duly paid on each deed in the chain must be called for.

Documents establishing the extent and the registration status of the estate must be called for; the estate is twenty acres, which is below the hundred-acre threshold, so a certificate of consent of the fragmentation Board is not required for this transfer.
Declarations of the agricultural landholdings of the vendor and of the shareholders of the purchaser company must be called for, so that the fifty-acre ceiling can be tested against both.
The purchaser's certificate of incorporation, articles, share register, register of directors and secretaries and a board resolution authorising the purchase must be called for.

Because thirty per cent of the purchaser's shares are held by a person who is not a citizen of Sri Lanka, a company secretary's certificate supported by the share register, showing foreign shareholding below fifty per cent, must be called for, failing which the Registrar of Lands will refuse registration.

The documents to be called for are the chain of notarial title deeds, a certified folio extract with certified copies of the registered instruments, the discharge of the registered bond, the survey plan and a current survey with possession evidence, proof of stamp duty on the chain, proof of the extent and registration status of the estate, declarations of agricultural landholdings, and the purchaser's corporate records including a secretary's certificate of foreign shareholding.
Examination on the papers alone is not sufficient here: the undischarged bond and the two acres held adversely must be resolved before the transfer is drawn.

enrichment.original_background: Lanka Rubber Trading (Private) Limited intents to purchase a Rubber Estate situated in Kalutara, Twenty Acres (A20-RO-PO) in extent. The said company instructs you to examine the title of the said Rubber Estate.
enrichment.enriched_background: Lanka Rubber Trading (Private) Limited intents to purchase a Rubber Estate situated in Kalutara, Twenty Acres (A20-RO-PO) in extent. The said company instructs you to examine the title of the said Rubber Estate. The company was incorporated in Sri Lanka in 2016 and carries on business at Colombo 03. Of its issued shares, thirty per cent are held by Mr. Tan Boon Heng, who resides in Singapore and is not a citizen of Sri Lanka, and the remaining seventy per cent by its two Sri Lankan directors. The estate is known as Rubberwatta, lying in the village of Bombuwala in the Kalutara District, and is depicted as Lot A in Plan No. 2143 dated 12 March 1998 made by K. Jayawardena, Licensed Surveyor. The proposed vendor is Mr. Sunil Weerakoon of Panadura, a citizen of Sri Lanka, who states that he became entitled to the entirety on Deed of Transfer No. 4562 attested on 8 June 2003 by W. D. Silva, Notary Public, and that his predecessor held on Deed of Gift No. 1120 attested on 2 February 1979. Mr. Weerakoon states that he owns no other agricultural land. The land is registered in the Kalutara Land Registry, and Mortgage Bond No. 987 dated 14 July 2016 in favour of a licensed commercial bank stands registered against it; Mr. Weerakoon says the loan has been settled but no discharge has been executed. A neighbour has fenced and occupied about two acres at the north-western corner of the estate for the last fifteen years and claims that portion as his own. Your instructions were given in October 2021.

added_facts.fact: Thirty per cent of the issued shares of Lanka Rubber Trading (Private) Limited are held by Mr. Tan Boon Heng, who resides in Singapore and is not a citizen of Sri Lanka; the remaining seventy per cent are held by its two Sri Lankan directors.
added_facts.reason: The original scenario says only that the purchaser is a private limited company. Whether the transfer is permitted at all turns on the level of foreign shareholding, so the shareholding has to be made determinate.
added_facts.counterfactual_effect: If the foreign shareholding were fifty per cent or above, the transfer of title would be prohibited and no amount of documentary examination would save it.

added_facts.fact: Lanka Rubber Trading (Private) Limited was incorporated in Sri Lanka in 2016 and carries on business at Colombo 03.
added_facts.reason: Fixes the purchaser as a locally incorporated company rather than a foreign company, which is the category the restriction on alienation of land distinguishes.
added_facts.counterfactual_effect: If the purchaser were incorporated outside Sri Lanka it would be a foreign company and the transfer would be prohibited outright.

added_facts.fact: The estate is known as Rubberwatta, lies in the village of Bombuwala in the Kalutara District, and is depicted as Lot A in Plan No. 2143 dated 12 March 1998 made by K. Jayawardena, Licensed Surveyor.
added_facts.reason: The original scenario identifies the property only by district and extent. A name, village and survey plan are needed before the description and boundary requirements can be applied.
added_facts.counterfactual_effect: Without an identified plan and locality the land could not be described by boundaries, extent and situation and no registrable deed could be drawn.

added_facts.fact: The proposed vendor is Mr. Sunil Weerakoon of Panadura, a citizen of Sri Lanka, who claims title on Deed of Transfer No. 4562 attested on 8 June 2003 by W. D. Silva, Notary Public, his predecessor having held on Deed of Gift No. 1120 attested on 2 February 1979.
added_facts.reason: The original scenario names no vendor and no instrument, so there is nothing on which a chain of title can be traced or a registry search framed.
added_facts.counterfactual_effect: If the vendor claimed on an unattested writing rather than on notarial deeds, he would have no title capable of transfer and the deeds called for would not establish title.

added_facts.fact: The land is registered in the Kalutara Land Registry and Mortgage Bond No. 987 dated 14 July 2016 in favour of a licensed commercial bank stands registered against it; the vendor says the loan has been settled but no discharge has been executed.
added_facts.reason: The original scenario gives no registration status and no encumbrance. A subsisting registered encumbrance is what makes the folio extract and the discharge decisive rather than formal.
added_facts.counterfactual_effect: If the folio were clear of encumbrances the purchaser would take free of any charge; with the bond undischarged on the register the purchaser takes subject to it.

added_facts.fact: A neighbour has fenced and occupied about two acres at the north-western corner of the estate for the last fifteen years and claims that portion as his own.
added_facts.reason: The original scenario is silent on possession. Adverse possession for more than ten years is capable of defeating the paper title to part of the estate, which is why possession evidence and a fresh survey are called for.
added_facts.counterfactual_effect: If the vendor were in undisturbed possession of the whole twenty acres, the paper title alone would answer and no separate possession inquiry would be needed.

added_facts.fact: Mr. Weerakoon states that he owns no other agricultural land.
added_facts.reason: Makes the agricultural landholding position determinate so that the ceiling on agricultural land can be applied to the vendor.
added_facts.counterfactual_effect: If the vendor owned agricultural land beyond the ceiling, part of his holding would be liable to vest and his title to the estate would be open to question.

added_facts.fact: The instructions to examine title were given in October 2021.
added_facts.reason: Anchors the examination to the matter reference date so that the law in force is not confused with later amendments.
added_facts.counterfactual_effect: A later date would bring in amendments to the notarial rules that were not in force when the instructions were given.

indispensable_provisions.formal_title: Registration of Title Act, No. 21 of 1998
indispensable_provisions.relevant_excerpt: No land parcel, title to which has been registered under this Act, or any interest therein shall be transferred or dealt with except in accordance with the provisions of this Act, and every disposition otherwise effected shall be void.
indispensable_provisions.why_relevant: The gate for the whole question. Because the land is registered under the Act, any gift of it, or of an interest in it, is valid only if it complies with the Act, and any other form of disposition is void. This is what turns the registrability rules in sections 46, 47 and 48 into conditions of validity rather than mere registry practice.
indispensable_provisions.temporal_note: In force from 1998 per the corpus; no amendment events recorded, so the text is treated as in force at 2021-10. The corpus edition is flagged original_or_unconfirmed_consolidation.

indispensable_provisions.formal_title: Registration of Title Act, No. 21 of 1998
indispensable_provisions.relevant_excerpt: The Registrar of Title shall not register any instrument which purports to convey any title or interest to a land parcel on the happening of any event, or the fulfilment of any condition at any future time: Provided however, that a conveyance of title subject to life interest shall be acceptable for registration.
indispensable_provisions.why_relevant: Answers the life-interest half of the question directly. A gift that reserves a life interest to the donor postpones the donees' full enjoyment, which would otherwise run into the bar on instruments conveying title on a future event or condition; the express proviso saves it and makes a conveyance subject to a life interest registrable.
indispensable_provisions.temporal_note: In force from 1998 per the corpus; no amendment events recorded, so the text is treated as in force at 2021-10.

indispensable_provisions.formal_title: Registration of Title Act, No. 21 of 1998
indispensable_provisions.relevant_excerpt: an instrument pertaining to the ownership of a land parcel registered under this Act, made in favour of two or more persons in common shall be void and shall not be registered under this Act.
indispensable_provisions.why_relevant: Answers the two-donees half of the question directly. A single deed of gift of one registered land parcel to two daughters in common is an instrument in favour of two or more persons in common, so it is void and unregistrable. The opening words, 'Except in accordance with the provisions of this Act', are what leave the sub-division route in sections 36 and 47 open.
indispensable_provisions.temporal_note: In force from 1998 per the corpus; no amendment events recorded, so the text is treated as in force at 2021-10.
indispensable_provisions.verifier_note: Wording confirmed verbatim, but the excerpt begins mid-sentence and drops the operative opening qualifier 'Except in accordance with the provisions of this Act,' on which the why_relevant relies; I checked that qualifier and it opens no route here, because the only co-ownership the Act itself creates arises from a declaration of the Commissioner of Title Settlement under section 14(d) on initial registration (sections 15 and 16), not from an instrument between parties.

indispensable_provisions.formal_title: Registration of Title Act, No. 21 of 1998
indispensable_provisions.relevant_excerpt: No part of a land parcel registered with a First Class Title of Absolute Ownership or a Second Class Title of Ownership under the provisions of this Act shall be transferred or otherwise dealt with unless the registered owner has first sub-divided such land parcel and the land parcel so subdivided has been registered under the provisions of this Act.
indispensable_provisions.why_relevant: Closes the obvious workaround of gifting a divided half to each daughter out of the existing parcel. No part of the registered parcel may be dealt with until the owner has sub-divided it and the sub-divided parcels are themselves registered, so sub-division must precede the gifts.
indispensable_provisions.temporal_note: In force from 1998 per the corpus; no amendment events recorded, so the text is treated as in force at 2021-10.

indispensable_provisions.formal_title: Registration of Title Act, No. 21 of 1998
indispensable_provisions.relevant_excerpt: Any owner or owners of any land parcel or land parcels whose title to which has been registered under this Act, may amalgamate or sub-divide his or their land parcel by registering a plan of redivision or amalgamation or sub-division relating to such land parcels in accordance with the provisions of this Act.
indispensable_provisions.why_relevant: Supplies the only route by which the donor's wish can be carried out. As registered owner he may sub-divide the parcel by registering a sub-division plan, after which each resulting land parcel is a separate unit of record that can be gifted to one daughter without offending the co-ownership bar.
indispensable_provisions.temporal_note: In force from 1998 per the corpus; no amendment events recorded, so the text is treated as in force at 2021-10.

indispensable_provisions.formal_title: Registration of Title Act, No. 21 of 1998
indispensable_provisions.relevant_excerpt: means a document having the effect of conveying title to and interest in any land parcel in the prescribed form, means an interest Jess than full ownership of the land parcel and includes any Servitudes or encumbrance over such land parcel
indispensable_provisions.why_relevant: Defines the two terms the answer turns on. A deed of gift is an 'instrument', a document having the effect of conveying title to and interest in a land parcel in the prescribed form, which is what brings it within sections 43, 46 and 48; and a reserved life interest is an 'interest in land parcel', an interest less than full ownership, which is what makes it a registrable interest rather than a bare condition.
indispensable_provisions.temporal_note: In force from 1998 per the corpus; no amendment events recorded. The corpus body of section 75 has lost the defined-term labels, so the excerpt reads as two run-on definitions; on the face of the Act these are the definitions of 'instrument' and of 'interest in land parcel', both listed in the corpus defined_terms for this section.
indispensable_provisions.verifier_note: The quoted text is verbatim, but the corpus body of section 75 has lost the defined-term labels and carries an OCR error ('Jess' for 'less'), so the excerpt is two run-on definitions; that the first is 'instrument' and the second 'interest in land parcel' follows from the section's recorded defined_terms order and from the use of 'instrument' in sections 43, 46 and 48, and is an inference from the corpus rather than something the corpus text states.

supporting_provisions.formal_title: Registration of Title Act, No. 21 of 1998
supporting_provisions.relevant_excerpt: Every instrument conveying title or any interest in a land parcel presented for registration under this Act shall be effected in the form prescribed for that purpose. (2) Instruments prepared under the provisions of subsection (1) shall be signed by the parties to the transaction and two witnesses and attested by a Notary Public
supporting_provisions.why_relevant: Fixes the form the deeds of gift must take: the prescribed form, signed by the parties and two witnesses and attested by a Notary Public. Goes to how the donor's wish is executed rather than to whether it can be achieved.
supporting_provisions.temporal_note: In force from 1998 per the corpus; no amendment events recorded. The prescribed form itself is made by regulation under section 67 and is not in the corpus.

supporting_provisions.formal_title: Registration of Title Act, No. 21 of 1998
supporting_provisions.relevant_excerpt: An instrument pertaining to land executed in accordance with the provisions of this Act shall take effect on registration, of such instrument under the provisions of this Act.
supporting_provisions.why_relevant: Timing rule: each deed of gift operates only when it is registered, not on execution or delivery, so the donor's wish is not fulfilled until registration is effected.
supporting_provisions.temporal_note: In force from 1998 per the corpus; no amendment events recorded.

supporting_provisions.formal_title: Registration of Title Act, No. 21 of 1998
supporting_provisions.relevant_excerpt: No person acquiring an interest in any land parcel registered under the provisions of this Act shall be entitled to such title or interest unless such title or interest is registered under the provisions of this Act.
supporting_provisions.why_relevant: Makes the same point from the donees' side: neither daughter is entitled to anything until her title is registered, and the donor's reserved life interest likewise has to appear on the register.
supporting_provisions.temporal_note: In force from 1998 per the corpus; no amendment events recorded.

supporting_provisions.formal_title: Registration of Title Act, No. 21 of 1998
supporting_provisions.relevant_excerpt: If the Registrar of Title is of the opinion that all requirements for registration under this Act are complied with, he shall register such title or interest in the prescribed manner
supporting_provisions.why_relevant: Shows registration is not automatic: the Registrar registers only if satisfied that the requirements of the Act are met, which is the practical checkpoint at which a single gift to two donees in common would be refused.
supporting_provisions.temporal_note: In force from 1998 per the corpus; no amendment events recorded.

legal_issues.issue: Whether a gift of a land parcel registered under the Registration of Title Act may reserve a life interest to the donor and still be registrable.
Whether one registered land parcel may be gifted by a single instrument to two donees in common.
Whether the donor may instead gift a divided portion of the parcel to each daughter, and what he must do first.
What form the gift must take and when it takes effect.

gold_answer_draft.issue: Whether Nimal Siriwardhana can carry out his wish to gift his land, registered under the Registration of Title Act No. 21 of 1998, to his two daughters while reserving a life interest to himself: that is, whether a deed of gift of the registered parcel to both daughters in common, subject to his life interest, can validly be made and registered, and if not, what he must do instead.
gold_answer_draft.rule: The land is a land parcel registered under the Registration of Title Act No. 21 of 1998, so section 39 applies: no registered land parcel or interest in it may be transferred or dealt with except in accordance with the Act, and every disposition otherwise effected is void. A deed of gift is an 'instrument' within section 75, a document having the effect of conveying title to and interest in a land parcel in the prescribed form, and a life interest is an 'interest in land parcel' under the same section, being an interest less than full ownership. On the life interest, section 46 forbids the Registrar of Title to register any instrument purporting to convey title or an interest on the happening of any event or the fulfilment of any condition at a future time, but the proviso to section 46 makes a conveyance of title subject to life interest acceptable for registration. On the two donees, section 48 provides that, except in accordance with the provisions of the Act, an instrument pertaining to the ownership of a registered land parcel made in favour of two or more persons in common is void and shall not be registered. Section 47 adds that no part of a parcel registered with a First Class Title of Absolute Ownership or a Second Class Title of Ownership may be transferred or otherwise dealt with unless the registered owner has first sub-divided it and the sub-divided parcel has itself been registered, and section 36(1) allows a registered owner to sub-divide by registering a sub-division plan in accordance with the Act. Any instrument must be in the prescribed form, signed by the parties and two witnesses and attested by a Notary Public under section 43; it is registered only if the Registrar of Title is satisfied that the requirements of the Act are met under section 45(3); it takes effect only on registration under section 49; and under section 38 no donee is entitled to any title or interest until it is registered.
gold_answer_draft.application: Nimal is the registered sole owner of a single land parcel with a First Class Title of Absolute Ownership, so section 39 governs everything he proposes to do with it. The reservation to himself of the right to live on the land and take its produce for the rest of his life is a life interest, an interest less than full ownership within section 75, and not a conveyance postponed to a future event or condition; a gift of the parcel subject to that reservation therefore falls within the proviso to section 46 and is acceptable for registration on that ground. The difficulty lies in the other half of the plan. He wants both daughters to take the whole parcel together in undivided equal half shares under one deed, which is an instrument pertaining to the ownership of a registered land parcel made in favour of two persons in common. Section 48 makes such an instrument void and directs that it shall not be registered, and under section 45(3) the Registrar of Title would refuse it; by section 49 it would in any event take effect only on registration, and by section 38 neither daughter would acquire anything. Nor can he sidestep this by gifting a divided half of the existing parcel to each daughter, because section 47 bars any dealing with part of a registered parcel until the owner has first sub-divided it and the sub-divided parcels have been registered, and on these facts the parcel has never been sub-divided and no sub-division plan has been surveyed or registered. What he can do is proceed under section 36(1): as registered owner he may apply to sub-divide the parcel and register a sub-division plan, and once each of the two resulting land parcels is registered he may execute a separate deed of gift of one parcel to each daughter, each gift reserving his life interest under the proviso to section 46, each in the prescribed form and attested by a Notary Public under section 43, and each taking effect on registration under section 49. Whether the forty-perch parcel can in fact be divided in two depends on the prescribed extent and on whether the area has been declared one in which the minimum economic unit principle applies under section 70, which cannot be determined on the facts given.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: Only in part, and not in the form he proposes. The life interest is no obstacle, because the proviso to section 46 expressly allows a conveyance of title subject to a life interest to be registered. But a single deed of gift of the one registered parcel to both daughters in common would be void and unregistrable under section 48, and a gift of a divided portion to each is barred by section 47 while the parcel remains unsub-divided. Nimal can achieve substantially what he wants only if he first sub-divides the parcel under section 36 and registers the sub-division, and then gifts one resulting parcel to each daughter by a separate instrument reserving his life interest, subject to the sub-division being permissible under the prescribed minimum extent for the area.

answer_claims.claim_text: Because the land is a land parcel registered under the Registration of Title Act, it may be transferred or dealt with only in accordance with that Act, and any disposition otherwise effected is void.
A deed of gift is an 'instrument' under the Act, and a life interest is an 'interest in land parcel', being an interest less than full ownership.

The Registrar of Title may not register an instrument purporting to convey title or an interest on a future event or condition, but a conveyance of title subject to a life interest is expressly acceptable for registration.

An instrument pertaining to the ownership of a registered land parcel made in favour of two or more persons in common is void and shall not be registered, except in accordance with the provisions of the Act.

No part of a parcel registered with a First Class Title of Absolute Ownership may be transferred or otherwise dealt with unless the registered owner has first sub-divided it and the sub-divided parcel has been registered.
A registered owner may sub-divide his land parcel by registering a sub-division plan in accordance with the Act.

Any such instrument must be in the prescribed form, signed by the parties and two witnesses and attested by a Notary Public; it is registered only if the Registrar of Title is satisfied that the Act's requirements are met, takes effect only on registration, and until registration confers no title or interest on the donees.

The right Nimal wishes to keep for the rest of his life, to live on the land and take its produce, is a life interest, so a gift of the parcel reserving it falls within the proviso to section 46 and is acceptable for registration on that ground.

A single deed of gift of the one registered parcel to both daughters in undivided equal half shares is an instrument in favour of two persons in common, so it would be void under section 48 and the Registrar of Title would refuse to register it.
Because the parcel has never been sub-divided and no sub-division plan has been registered, he cannot instead gift a divided half of the existing parcel to each daughter.

He may first apply to sub-divide the parcel and register a sub-division plan, and once each resulting land parcel is registered he may gift one parcel to each daughter by a separate notarially attested instrument reserving his life interest, each gift taking effect on registration.

Whether the forty-perch parcel can in fact be divided in two depends on the prescribed extent and on whether the area has been declared one in which the minimum economic unit principle applies, which cannot be determined on the facts given.

Nimal cannot fulfil his desire in the form he proposes: the reservation of a life interest is permissible, but a single gift of the registered parcel to both daughters in common is void and unregistrable, and a gift of divided portions is barred while the parcel remains unsub-divided.

He can achieve substantially what he wants by first sub-dividing the parcel and registering the sub-division, and then gifting one resulting parcel to each daughter subject to his life interest, provided the sub-division is permissible under the prescribed minimum extent for the area.

enrichment.original_background: Nimal Siriwardhana wishes to gift his property registered under the Registration Title Act No.21 of 1998 to his two daughters subject to life interest of him.
enrichment.enriched_background: Nimal Siriwardhana wishes to gift his property registered under the Registration Title Act No.21 of 1998 to his two daughters subject to life interest of him. The property is a single land parcel of about forty perches at Meegoda, in the Homagama Divisional Secretary's Division of the Colombo District, separately delineated as Parcel No. 214 on the cadastral map for that area and entered in the Title Register kept at the Homagama Title Registry, where Nimal is recorded as the sole owner with a First Class Title of Absolute Ownership and no encumbrance stands registered against the parcel. His daughters, Kanchana Siriwardhana and Dilini Siriwardhana, are both over eighteen years of age. Nimal wants the two of them to take the whole parcel together, in undivided equal half shares, under one deed of gift, and he intends to keep for himself, for the rest of his life, the right to live on the land and to take its produce. The parcel has never been sub-divided; no sub-division plan of it has been surveyed or registered, and Nimal has made no application to the Registrar of Title to sub-divide it. He proposes to have the deed drawn and attested by a notary public in October 2021.

added_facts.fact: The property is one land parcel, separately delineated as Parcel No. 214 on the cadastral map for the area, and Nimal is recorded in the Title Register at the Homagama Title Registry as its sole owner with a First Class Title of Absolute Ownership, with no encumbrance registered against it.
added_facts.reason: The question says only that the property is registered under the Act. Whether it is one parcel or several, and whether the title is a First Class Title of Absolute Ownership, decides whether the co-ownership bar and the part-parcel bar bite at all. Naming the parcel and the registry also settles the property identity the classification flagged as missing.
added_facts.counterfactual_effect: If the property were already two separate registered parcels he could simply gift one parcel to each daughter subject to his life interest and the co-ownership bar would never be engaged. If it were not registered under this Act at all, the question would fall to be answered under the general law of gifts instead.

added_facts.fact: The parcel is about forty perches in extent and lies at Meegoda, in the Homagama Divisional Secretary's Division of the Colombo District.
added_facts.reason: Supplies the property location the classification flagged as missing and gives the parcel an extent, so the sub-division route can be discussed as a realistic option rather than in the abstract.
added_facts.counterfactual_effect: A much smaller extent, or an area declared subject to the minimum economic unit principle, could make a two-way sub-division unregistrable and leave the donor with no lawful way to benefit both daughters in his lifetime.

added_facts.fact: The two daughters are Kanchana Siriwardhana and Dilini Siriwardhana, both over eighteen years of age.
added_facts.reason: Supplies the party identity the classification flagged as missing and removes any minority or capacity side-issue, so the answer turns on the registration rules alone.
added_facts.counterfactual_effect: If a daughter were a minor, questions of capacity and of who accepts and presents the instrument would arise alongside the registration rules; the co-ownership bar would still apply.

added_facts.fact: Nimal wants both daughters to take the whole parcel together in undivided equal half shares under one deed of gift; the parcel has never been sub-divided, no sub-division plan has been surveyed or registered, and he has made no application to the Registrar of Title to sub-divide it.
added_facts.reason: The question does not say whether the daughters are to take jointly in undivided shares or a divided portion each. That is the fact the answer turns on, and the absence of any sub-division is what makes the divided-portion alternative unavailable as things stand.
added_facts.counterfactual_effect: Had he already sub-divided the parcel into two registered parcels, a separate gift of one parcel to each daughter subject to his life interest would be registrable and his wish could be carried out at once.

added_facts.fact: Nimal intends to keep for himself, for the rest of his life, the right to live on the land and to take its produce, and proposes to have the deed drawn and attested by a notary public in October 2021.
added_facts.reason: Spells out that the reservation is a life interest in the donor and not a condition or a gift taking effect on a future event, which is the distinction the rule on future conveyances turns on. It also fixes the date of the intended transaction at the matter reference date.
added_facts.counterfactual_effect: If the deed were framed so that title passed to the daughters only on the donor's death or on some other future event, it could not be registered at all, and the proviso saving conveyances subject to a life interest would not help him.

indispensable_provisions.why_relevant: Establishes that an agreement affecting immovable property, other than a lease at will or for a period not exceeding one month, has no force in law unless it is in writing and notarially attested. A four-year lease of the Colombo building therefore requires a notary at all.

Both post-date the matter. The corpus carries the consolidated post-2024 text, so the execution formalities shown in the corpus body are not the text in force in October 2021, but the lease carve-out relied on here is.

indispensable_provisions.relevant_excerpt: He shall not authenticate or attest any deed or instrument in any area other than that in which he is authorized to practice, nor in any language other than that in which he is authorized to practice nor authenticate or attest any deed or instrument drawn in any language other than that in which he is authorized to practice.
indispensable_provisions.why_relevant: The only territorial and language limit on a notary's competence to attest. It restricts the area in which the notary may act and the language of the instrument; it says nothing about where the land affected by the instrument is situated.
indispensable_provisions.temporal_note: Rule (22) is not among the rules substituted, inserted or repealed by the Notaries (Amendment) Act No. 31 of 2022 s.16 or by Act No. 6 of 2024 s.3, so the text shown is the text in force at 2021-10.

indispensable_provisions.relevant_excerpt: If a deed or instrument other than a will or codicil affects a land situated in a district other than that in which the notary before whom it is signed, and by whom it is attested, 'shall reside, such notary, or in case such deed or instrument is attested by two or more notaries, then the notary upon whom is cast the duty of transmitting to the Registrar of Lands the duplicate of such deed or instrument, shall on or before the fifteenth day of the month next following that in which the same was executed (besides transmitting the duplicate in manner aforesaid) deliver or transmit to the Registrar of Lands of the district in which such land shall be situated a copy thereof certified by him as correct

It is the provision that answers the Galle notary and Colombo building point.
indispensable_provisions.temporal_note: Rule (29) is not among the rules substituted, inserted or repealed by the Notaries (Amendment) Act No. 31 of 2022 s.16 or by Act No. 6 of 2024 s.3, so the text shown is the text in force at 2021-10.
indispensable_provisions.verifier_note: Wording and role confirmed, but the temporal_note is wrong on one point: 6-2024 s.3(9) did amend rule (29), substituting "in the Form F 1" for "in the Form F"; that amendment falls outside the quoted excerpt, so the substance relied on was in force at 2021-10 and the conclusion is unaffected.

supporting_provisions.relevant_excerpt: Every warrant issued to a notary under the provisions of section 3* or section 4* authorizing him to practice as a notary in any judicial division in which he resides, shall be deemed to authorize him to practice as a notary in the judicial zone in which he resides.
