legal_issues.issue: Whether a lease of a commercial building for four years must be executed before and attested by a notary at all.

Whether a notary whose warrant authorises him to practise in the Galle area is competent to attest a lease of a building situated in Colombo, that is, whether the statutory limit attaches to the place of attestation or to the situation of the land.
Whether the notary is disqualified because the lessor is his neighbour, and whether the lessor's illiteracy prevents him from attesting.

gold_answer_draft.issue: Whether Kamal Rathnayaka, a notary practising in Galle, may lawfully attest a four-year lease of a commercial building situated in Colombo granted by his neighbour Sudath Gunawardana, who is illiterate, to Kapila Warnakulasooriya.
gold_answer_draft.rule: Under Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.2 no agreement affecting immovable property, other than a lease at will or for a period not exceeding one month, is of force in law unless it is in writing and attested by a notary. Notaries Ordinance s.31 rule (22) provides that a notary shall not authenticate or attest any deed or instrument in any area other than that in which he is authorized to practice, nor in any language other than that in which he is authorized to practice. Notaries Ordinance s.4A deems a warrant issued for a judicial division to authorise practice in the judicial zone in which the notary resides, and s.9 binds him to have his office within the area specified in his warrant. The limit is therefore on where the notary acts, not on where the land lies: s.31 rule (29) expressly contemplates a deed or instrument affecting land situated in a district other than that in which the attesting notary resides, and requires him to deliver or transmit to the Registrar of Lands of the district in which the land is situated a certified copy, on or before the fifteenth day of the following month. As to personal capacity, s.31 rule (13) disqualifies a notary only from attesting a deed or instrument to which he is a party. Where an executant is or professes to be unable to read the instrument, s.31 rule (11) forbids attestation unless and until the notary has read over and explained it, or caused it to be explained, in the presence and hearing of that person and in the presence of the attesting witnesses.
gold_answer_draft.application: The proposed lease is for four years, far beyond the one month carved out of Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.2, so it must be in writing and notarially attested to be of any force in law. Kamal Rathnayaka holds a notarial warrant and practises in Galle. Nothing in the Notaries Ordinance ties his competence to the district in which the leased property stands: s.31 rule (22) looks only to the area and the language in which he is authorized to practice, and s.4A extends that area to the judicial zone in which he resides. Provided the lease is drawn in a language in which he is authorized to practice and is executed and attested by him within that area, rule (22) is satisfied even though the building is in Colombo. That the land is in another district is dealt with expressly by rule (29), which assumes the attestation is good and adds a duty to send a certified copy to the Registrar of Lands of the Colombo district within the prescribed time. Kamal is Sudath Gunawardana's neighbour but he is not a party to the lease, which is between Sudath as lessor and Kapila Warnakulasooriya as lessee, so rule (13) does not touch him; his acquaintance with the lessor in fact assists identification. Sudath's illiteracy is likewise not a bar: it engages rule (11) and obliges Kamal to read over and explain the lease to him, in his presence and hearing and in the presence of the attesting witnesses, before attestation.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: Yes. Kamal Rathnayaka can attest this lease agreement, and the lease in fact needs notarial attestation to be of force in law. His competence turns not on the Colombo situation of the building but on the execution and attestation taking place within the area, and the instrument being in a language, authorised by his warrant. The Colombo location affects only his later duty under s.31 rule (29) to transmit a certified copy to the Registrar of Lands of that district; his relationship as neighbour is no disqualification under rule (13); and the lessor's illiteracy obliges him to comply with rule (11) rather than to decline the work. Were the lease to be signed and attested outside the area of his warrant, or drawn in a language he is not authorised to practise in, the answer would be no.

answer_claims.claim_text: An agreement affecting immovable property, other than a lease at will or for a period not exceeding one month, is of no force in law unless it is in writing and notarially attested.

A notary must not authenticate or attest any deed or instrument in any area other than that in which he is authorized to practice, nor in any language other than that in which he is authorized to practice.

A warrant authorising a notary to practise in a judicial division is deemed to authorise him to practise in the judicial zone in which he resides, and he must keep his office within the area specified in his warrant.

The Notaries Ordinance contemplates a notary attesting an instrument that affects land situated in a district other than the district in which he resides, and requires him in that case to deliver or transmit a certified copy to the Registrar of Lands of the district in which the land is situated on or before the fifteenth day of the following month.
A notary is disqualified from attesting only a deed or instrument to which he is himself a party.

Where an executant is or professes to be unable to read the instrument, the notary must not attest it unless and until he has read over and explained it, or caused it to be explained, in the presence and hearing of that executant and in the presence of the attesting witnesses.
Because the proposed lease runs for four years it falls outside the one month carve-out and must be notarially attested to be of force in law.

That the building is in Colombo while Kamal Rathnayaka practises in Galle does not affect his competence to attest, because the statutory limit attaches to the area in which he attests and not to the situation of the land.

Because the leased land is in a district other than the district in which Kamal Rathnayaka resides, he must in addition transmit a certified copy of the lease to the Registrar of Lands of the Colombo district.
Kamal Rathnayaka is a neighbour of the lessor but not a party to the lease, so rule (13) does not disqualify him.
Sudath Gunawardana's illiteracy does not bar attestation but obliges the notary to read over and explain the lease to him in the presence of the attesting witnesses before it is attested.
Kamal Rathnayaka can attest this lease agreement, provided the execution and attestation take place within the area, and the instrument is in a language, authorised by his warrant.
Were the lease signed and attested outside the area of his warrant, or drawn in a language he is not authorised to practise in, he could not lawfully attest it.

enrichment.original_background: Kamal Rathnayaka is a Notary practicing in Galle. Sudath Gunawardana is a neighbour of Kamal Ratnayake and the owner of a commercial building in Colombo. indispensable_provisions.relevant_excerpt: (1) It shall be the duty of every notary to endeavour to ascertain the true and full consideration for the execution of any deed, and to insert and set forth the same in such deed. (2) Any notary who shall knowingly and willfully insert or set forth in or upon any such deed any other than the full and true consideration or money directly or indirectly paid or secured, or agreed to be paid or secured for the same, or the actual value of the same, or shall abet the doing thereof, respectively, shall be guilty of an offence
indispensable_provisions.why_relevant: The central provision for the request to understate the rental. Subsection (1) puts the notary under a positive duty to ascertain and set out the true and full consideration; subsection (2) makes knowingly inserting anything other than the full and true consideration, or abetting it, an offence with civil liability in addition.
indispensable_provisions.temporal_note: Subsection (1) has stood since 1907. The Notaries (Amendment) Act No. 31 of 2022 s.18 amended subsection (2) only by substituting the words "not exceeding fifty thousand rupees" for "not exceeding twenty five thousand rupees". The excerpt stops before the penalty words, so the quoted text was in force at 2021-10; the maximum fine at that date was twenty five thousand rupees, not the fifty thousand shown in the corpus body.
indispensable_provisions.verifier_note: Temporal analysis checked against 31-2022 s.18, which substituted "not exceeding fifty thousand rupees" for "not exceeding twenty five thousand rupees" in subsection (2) only; the excerpt stops before the penalty words. 6-2024 s.4 inserted s.38A and did not touch s.38.

indispensable_provisions.why_relevant: Inserting a rental figure the notary knows to be false, with intent to defeat the revenue, falls within paragraph (b) and exposes him to the heavier penalty for fraud in the execution of his office, over and above the section 38 offence.
indispensable_provisions.temporal_note: Paragraph (b) was not amended in 2022. The Notaries (Amendment) Act No. 31 of 2022 s.19 amended paragraph (c) and substituted the closing penalty words, so that imprisonment "not exceeding five years" became ten years with a fine and compensation. The excerpt is confined to paragraph (b) and was in force at 2021-10; the penalty at that date was imprisonment not exceeding five years.
indispensable_provisions.verifier_note: Temporal analysis checked against 31-2022 s.19, which amended paragraph (c) and the closing penalty words only; paragraph (b) is unchanged.

legal_issues.issue: Whether the lease agreement is chargeable with stamp duty and on whom the duty falls, so that understating the rental would reduce the duty payable.
What duty the Notaries Ordinance imposes on the notary as to the consideration to be inserted in the instrument, and whether he may accede to the parties' request.
What criminal, civil and professional liabilities the notary incurs if he inserts the lower rental, and what he must do instead.

gold_answer_draft.issue: What are the duties and the liabilities of Kamal Rathnayaka as a notary when the lessor and the lessee ask him to insert in the lease agreement a rental lower than the agreed Rs. 60,000 per month in order to reduce the stamp duty payable.
gold_answer_draft.rule: A lease or hire of any property is a specified instrument under Stamp Duty (Special Provisions) Act s.4, and by s.3 stamp duty is charged on every specified instrument executed, drawn or presented in Sri Lanka at the rate the Minister determines by Order published in the Gazette; by s.6 the duty on a lease is payable by the lessee unless there is agreement to the contrary. Notaries Ordinance s.38(1) makes it the duty of every notary to endeavour to ascertain the true and full consideration for the execution of any deed and to insert and set forth the same in the deed, and s.38(2) makes a notary who knowingly and wilfully inserts anything other than the full and true consideration, or abets the doing of it, guilty of an offence and liable to a fine in addition to any civil liability he may incur. Notaries Ordinance s.39(b) further provides that a notary who knowingly and wilfully, with intent to prejudice or defraud any person, inserts in any deed or instrument any figure or thing which ought not to have been inserted, or omits any which ought to have been inserted, is guilty of an offence carrying imprisonment. Notaries Ordinance s.31 rule (20)(f) requires the attestation itself to state the number and value of the stamps affixed to the instrument and to its duplicate. Understating the consideration does not defeat the revenue in any event: under Stamp Duty (Special Provisions) Act s.10 an Assessor who is of opinion that an instrument liable to stamp duty has not been duly stamped shall assess the duty payable and require the person liable to pay it. Beyond the criminal law, Notaries Ordinance s.21(1) makes gross misconduct in the discharge of notarial duties, and repeated breaches of the rules under the Ordinance, grounds on which a report may be made to the Minister, who may suspend the notary or cancel his warrant.
gold_answer_draft.application: The agreed rental is Rs. 60,000 per month for four years, so that is the true and full consideration for the lease. The lease is a specified instrument chargeable with stamp duty at the rate in force, and the duty ordinarily falls on Kapila Warnakulasooriya as lessee. If Kamal Rathnayaka writes a lower rental into the lease at the parties' request, he inserts something other than the full and true consideration knowing it to be false, which is what s.38(2) forbids, and the same act would abet the parties' own attempt to underpay. Because the object stated by the parties is to save stamp duty, the false figure would be inserted with intent to prejudice the revenue, which brings the conduct within s.39(b) as well. He would also be certifying in his own attestation, under rule (20)(f), a stamp value corresponding to a figure he knows to be untrue. The parties gain nothing lawful by the exercise, since an Assessor may in any event assess the duty properly payable and require the lessee to pay it. Kamal Rathnayaka's duty is therefore to ascertain and insert the true rental of Rs. 60,000 per month, to explain to the parties that he cannot record any other figure, and to decline to execute the lease on the terms proposed if they persist.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: Kamal Rathnayaka must refuse the request. His duty under Notaries Ordinance s.38(1) is to ascertain the true and full consideration and to set it forth in the instrument, which here means the agreed rental of Rs. 60,000 per month. If he accedes he commits an offence under s.38(2), punishable by a fine and leaving him civilly liable in addition, and, because the figure would be inserted with intent to defeat the stamp duty, a further and graver offence under s.39(b) punishable with imprisonment. He would also expose himself to inquiry for gross misconduct under s.21, on a report of which the Minister may suspend him or cancel his warrant. The proper course is to record the true rental, satisfy himself that the correct stamp duty is provided, state the stamp particulars accurately in his attestation, and refuse to attest the lease if the parties insist on the false figure.

answer_claims.claim_text: A lease or hire of any property is a specified instrument chargeable with stamp duty at the rate determined by the Minister by Order published in the Gazette.
In the case of a lease the stamp duty is payable by the lessee, otherwise than where there is an agreement to the contrary.
It is the duty of every notary to endeavour to ascertain the true and full consideration for the execution of a deed and to insert and set it forth in the deed.

A notary who knowingly and wilfully inserts other than the full and true consideration, or abets the doing of it, is guilty of an offence and is liable in addition to any civil liability he may incur.
A notary who knowingly and wilfully, with intent to prejudice or defraud any person, inserts in an instrument a figure which ought not to have been inserted commits a further offence.
The attestation must state the number and value of the adhesive stamps affixed to, or the value of the impressed stamps on, the instrument and its duplicate.
Where an Assessor is of opinion that an instrument liable to stamp duty has not been duly stamped he shall assess the duty payable and require the person liable to pay it.

Gross misconduct in the discharge of notarial duties, or repeated breaches of the rules under the Ordinance, are grounds for inquiry and for a report on which the Minister may suspend the notary or cancel his warrant.
The true and full consideration for this lease is the agreed monthly rental of Rs. 60,000 over the four-year term, and that is the figure the notary is bound to insert.
Inserting a lower rental at the parties' request would be knowingly and wilfully setting forth other than the full and true consideration, and would also abet the parties' underpayment of duty.
Because the stated object is to save stamp duty, the false figure would be inserted with intent to prejudice the revenue and would fall within the fraud provision as well.
The notary would additionally be certifying in his own attestation a stamp value corresponding to a rental he knows to be untrue.
The understatement would not in any event defeat the duty, since an Assessor may assess the duty properly payable on the lease and require the lessee to pay it.
Kamal Rathnayaka must refuse the request, ascertain and insert the true rental of Rs. 60,000 per month, and decline to attest the lease if the parties insist on the false figure.

If he accedes he commits an offence under section 38(2) of the Notaries Ordinance with civil liability in addition, and a further offence under section 39(b), and exposes himself to inquiry for gross misconduct on which the Minister may suspend him or cancel his warrant.

indispensable_provisions.why_relevant: This is the operative penal provision. It makes acting as a notary without the yearly certificate an offence, and it makes the offence bite in respect of every deed executed or acknowledged before the notary while he was uncertificated, which is exactly the lease Kamal Ratnayake attested.
indispensable_provisions.temporal_note: In force from 1907. The only recorded change is the fine increase by the Increase of Fines Act No. 12 of 2005, which is in force well before 2021-10; the Rs. 5,000 to Rs. 25,000 range therefore applies at the matter date.

indispensable_provisions.relevant_excerpt: All such certificates shall be applied for and granted on or before the first day of April in every year, and shall be in force for one year and no longer: Provided, however, that if such certificate shall not be applied for within the time limited, and it shall be shown to the satisfaction of the High Court Judge that the delay was due to accident, misfortune or other unavoidable cause, the High Court Judge may direct the Registrar to issue the required certificate notwithstanding such delay as aforesaid.
indispensable_provisions.why_relevant: Section 30 punishes acting without "such certificate as aforesaid"; s.27 is what that phrase refers to. It creates the yearly certificate issued by the Registrar of the High Court of the zone, fixes the annual application deadline, limits the certificate to one year, and supplies the only statutory relief for a notary who missed the deadline through accident, misfortune or other unavoidable cause.
indispensable_provisions.temporal_note: In force from 1907. Subsection (3) was substituted by Notaries (Amendment) Act No. 13 of 2013 s.2 (before the matter date). Subsection (2) was later amended by Notaries (Amendment) Act No. 31 of 2022 s.14, which substituted "April" for "March"; that change post-dates 2021-10, so at the matter date the deadline was the first day of March. The excerpt is taken from the consolidated corpus text and so shows "April". Nothing in the answer turns on which month it was: the notary obtained no certificate at all for the year.
indispensable_provisions.verifier_note: Excerpt verified verbatim, but it reproduces the post-matter wording: 31-2022 s.14 substituted "April" for "March" in subsection (2), so at 2021-10 the deadline read the first day of March, and the corpus holds no as-at-2021 snapshot; the excerpt also covers subsection (2) only, while claim CL-M057-Q01-001 additionally rests on the subsection (1) duty of the Registrar of the High Court to issue the certificate.

supporting_provisions.relevant_excerpt: the Registrar-General may, if he thinks fit, instead of instituting criminal proceedings against such notary, accept from him such sum of money as he may consider proper in composition of the offence
supporting_provisions.why_relevant: Section 35(1) names s.30 among the compoundable offences, so the liability is not necessarily a prosecution: the Registrar-General may accept a sum in composition, after which criminal proceedings shall not be taken or continued. It qualifies how the s.30 liability may be discharged.
supporting_provisions.temporal_note: In force from 1907 with no recorded amendment events, so the text applies unchanged at 2021-10.

supporting_provisions.relevant_excerpt: Where the report is to the effect that the notary has been guilty of any such offence or misconduct as is mentioned in clauses (a), (b), (c), or (d) of the last preceding subsection, the Minister may cancel the warrant of such notary, or may suspend him from office for such period as may appear just.
supporting_provisions.why_relevant: Beyond the fine, an offence committed in the capacity of a notary opens the disciplinary route: on a report by the High Court Judge after inquiry under s.21(1), the Minister may cancel the warrant or suspend the notary. This is a possible further liability, not an automatic one, so it is supporting rather than indispensable.
supporting_provisions.temporal_note: In force from 1907. Notaries (Amendment) Act No. 31 of 2022 s.11 substituted parts of the section after the matter date; the subsection (2) power to cancel or suspend relied on here is long-standing, but a verifier should confirm the 2022 substitution did not touch the quoted words before treating the excerpt as the as-at-2021 text. Marked supporting for that reason.
supporting_provisions.verifier_note: Verifier resolved the researcher's open point: 31-2022 s.11 amends only s.21(1)(e) ("incompetence, age" to "incompetence") and s.21(4) (fine), so the quoted subsection (2) is unchanged as-at-2021 text; the supporting rather than indispensable role is nonetheless correct, since s.21(2) bites only on a High Court Judge's report under s.21(1).

legal_issues.issue: Whether a notary who attests a deed during a year for which he has not obtained the certificate issued yearly by the Registrar of the High Court commits an offence, and what penalty attaches.
Whether the penalty runs per deed attested while uncertificated, and whether the offence can be compounded instead of prosecuted.
Whether any relief remains open to the notary for the missed certificate, and what further professional consequence the lapse may carry.

gold_answer_draft.issue: What liability does Kamal Ratnayake incur for having attested the four-year lease of Sudath Gunawardana's commercial building at a time when he had not obtained, for the current year, the certificate issued to notaries by the Registrar of the High Court?
gold_answer_draft.rule: Notaries Ordinance s.27 requires every notary to apply for and obtain from the Registrar of the High Court of his zone a certificate that he is a notary duly authorised to practise there. Such certificates must be applied for and granted on or before the annual date fixed by s.27(2) and are in force for one year and no longer, so a fresh certificate is needed each year. Where the application was not made within the time limited, s.27(2) allows the High Court Judge, if satisfied that the delay was due to accident, misfortune or other unavoidable cause, to direct the Registrar to issue the certificate notwithstanding the delay. Section 30 provides that any person who acts as a notary without having obtained such certificate is guilty of an offence in respect of every deed executed or acknowledged before him as such notary while he was without the certificate, and is liable to a fine of not less than Rs. 5,000 and not exceeding Rs. 25,000. Under s.35(1) the offence under s.30 is compoundable: the Registrar-General may, instead of instituting criminal proceedings, accept such sum as he considers proper in composition, after which criminal proceedings shall not be taken or continued. Separately, where the High Court Judge reports after inquiry under s.21 that a notary has been guilty of an offence rendering him unfit, or of gross misconduct in the discharge of his duties, s.21(2) empowers the Minister to cancel his warrant or suspend him from office. Section 13, the offence of practising without a warrant, declaration, bond or filed copy of the warrant, is a different matter and is not engaged where the notary holds a warrant.
gold_answer_draft.application: The lease is of a commercial building for four years, well outside the Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.2 exception for a lease at will or for a period not exceeding one month, so it had to be executed before and attested by a notary; Kamal Ratnayake was accordingly acting in his capacity as a notary when he attested it. On his own recollection he had not obtained the yearly certificate under s.27 for the current year, and a certificate for an earlier year would in any event have expired, being in force for one year and no longer. He therefore acted as a notary without having obtained such certificate, and the lease is a deed executed before him as such notary while he was uncertificated, which is precisely what s.30 penalises. The penalty attaches in respect of every such deed, so the lease attracts one offence and any other deed he attested during the uncertificated period attracts its own. Whether the Registrar-General prosecutes or instead accepts a sum in composition under s.35(1) is a matter for the Registrar-General's discretion. If Kamal Ratnayake can show that his failure to apply in time was due to accident, misfortune or other unavoidable cause he may still ask the High Court Judge under the proviso to s.27(2) to direct the Registrar to issue the certificate, but that relief goes to obtaining the certificate late and does not undo an offence already committed by attesting while uncertificated. On the facts given, mere forgetfulness is not stated to be accident, misfortune or unavoidable cause, so the availability of that relief is open.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: Kamal Ratnayake is guilty of an offence under s.30 of the Notaries Ordinance in respect of the lease he attested while without the yearly certificate required by s.27, and is liable to a fine of not less than Rs. 5,000 and not exceeding Rs. 25,000 for that deed, with a further such liability for each other deed attested during the uncertificated period. The Registrar-General may compound the offence under s.35(1) instead of prosecuting. He may apply under the proviso to s.27(2) for the certificate to be issued despite his delay if the delay was due to accident, misfortune or other unavoidable cause. He also stands exposed, on a s.21 inquiry and report, to cancellation of his warrant or suspension from office by the Minister. He is not liable under s.13, which addresses practising without a warrant.

answer_claims.claim_text: Every notary must obtain from the Registrar of the High Court a yearly certificate, applied for and granted by the annual date fixed by s.27(2), which is in force for one year and no longer.

A person who acts as a notary without having obtained that certificate is guilty of an offence in respect of every deed executed or acknowledged before him as such notary while he was without it, and is liable to a fine of not less than Rs. 5,000 and not exceeding Rs. 25,000.
The Registrar-General may, instead of instituting criminal proceedings for an offence under s.30, accept a sum in composition, after which criminal proceedings shall not be taken or continued.
Where the High Court Judge reports after inquiry that a notary has been guilty of an offence or misconduct within s.21(1)(a) to (d), the Minister may cancel his warrant or suspend him from office.
A lease of immovable property for four years is not within the exception for a lease at will or for a period not exceeding one month, so it had to be executed before and attested by a notary.
Kamal Ratnayake attested the four-year lease in his capacity as a notary at a time when he had not obtained the yearly certificate for the current year.
The lease is therefore a deed executed before him as a notary while he was without the certificate, which is the conduct s.30 penalises, and the penalty runs separately in respect of each such deed.

The proviso to s.27(2) may still allow him to obtain the certificate late if the delay was due to accident, misfortune or other unavoidable cause, but that relief does not undo an offence already committed by attesting while uncertificated, and the background states only that he forgot.
He is not liable under s.13, which penalises practising without a warrant, declaration, bond or filed copy of the warrant, since he holds a warrant and lacks only the yearly certificate.

Kamal Ratnayake is guilty of an offence under s.30 of the Notaries Ordinance and liable to a fine of not less than Rs. 5,000 and not exceeding Rs. 25,000 in respect of the lease, with a further such liability for each other deed attested during the uncertificated period.

That liability may be discharged by composition accepted by the Registrar-General rather than by prosecution, and he additionally risks cancellation of his warrant or suspension from office by the Minister following a s.21 inquiry and report.

indispensable_provisions.relevant_excerpt: Where at the time of the execution of a mortgage bond in favour of a lending institution for the payment of a loan, the principal of which exceeds one hundred and fifty thousand rupees the mortgagor executes a separate instrument, attested by the notary attesting the bond and by the witnesses to the bond containing- (a) a special declaration on the part of the mortgagor that he renounces the benefit of section 46 and that the effect of such renunciation has been explained to him by the notary
indispensable_provisions.why_relevant: This is the provision the Bank's requested declaration is executed under. It is the only route by which a mortgagor's property other than the mortgaged land can be made liable under a decree on the mortgage: a separate instrument, executed at the time of the bond, containing a special declaration renouncing the benefit of section 46. It also sets the two gateway conditions - a lending institution as mortgagee and a loan principal exceeding Rs.150,000.
indispensable_provisions.temporal_note: Inserted by Act No. 3 of 1990 and in force from 1990; no later amendment event is recorded on this section in the corpus. It is therefore in force at the matter reference date of October 2021. Subsection (6) excludes mortgages created before the section came into force, which does not affect a mortgage to be created in 2021.

indispensable_provisions.relevant_excerpt: No decree in any hypothecary action upon any mortgage of land which is created after the coming into force of this section, and no decree in any action for the recovery of any moneys due upon any such mortgage, shall order any property, whatsoever, other than the mortgaged property to be sold for the recovery of any money found to be due under the mortgage, and no property whatsoever, other than the mortgaged property, shall be sold or be liable to be sold in execution of any such decree.
indispensable_provisions.why_relevant: This is the benefit that the s.47A declaration renounces, and it explains the Bank's motive. Without a renunciation the Bank's recovery on a decree is confined to the mortgaged Rajagiriya land; if that land realises less than the debt, the shortfall cannot be recovered against the mortgagor's other property.
indispensable_provisions.temporal_note: Substituted by Act No. 3 of 1990; latest recorded change 1990, so the substituted text is the text in force at October 2021.

indispensable_provisions.temporal_note: Part of s.47A as inserted in 1990; no later amendment event recorded. The footnote reference to section 2 of Act No. 23 of 1997 in paragraph (e) concerns the DFCC Bank only and does not bear on paragraph (d).

indispensable_provisions.relevant_excerpt: then, in addition to the mortgaged property, any other property belonging to the mortgagor shall, subject To the provisions of subsection(2), be liable to be ordered to be sold and to be sold under the decree in an action upon the mortgage, and the provisions of section 218 of the Civil Procedure Code (Chapter 101) shall, mutatis mutandis, apply to the seizure and sale of such other property.

indispensable_provisions.temporal_note: Same insertion by Act No. 3 of 1990; in force at October 2021. The corpus text reproduces the printed capitalisation 'subject To' and the unspaced 'subsection(2)'.

legal_issues.issue: What, under the Mortgage Act, is the legal effect of a mortgagor executing a separate declaration under section 47A at the execution of a mortgage bond?
What is the default position under section 46 that such a declaration renounces, and can a lender achieve the same result without it?
Are the statutory gateway conditions of section 47A satisfied on these facts, namely a lending institution as mortgagee and a loan principal exceeding one hundred and fifty thousand rupees?

gold_answer_draft.issue: Why does the National Savings Bank ask Lihini Manapitiya to execute a separate declaration under section 47A of the Mortgage Act at the time she mortgages her Rajagiriya land to secure the Rs.2,000,000 housing loan?
gold_answer_draft.rule: Mortgage Act s.46 provides that no decree in a hypothecary action on a mortgage of land, and no decree in an action for the recovery of moneys due on such a mortgage, may order any property other than the mortgaged property to be sold, and no other property is liable to be sold in execution of such a decree. By s.47 that restriction operates notwithstanding anything in any other law or in any mortgage bond or other instrument, so a lender cannot escape it by a clause in the bond. Section 47A creates the single statutory exception. Where, at the time of execution of a mortgage bond in favour of a lending institution for a loan the principal of which exceeds one hundred and fifty thousand rupees, the mortgagor executes a separate instrument attested by the notary attesting the bond and by the witnesses to it, containing a special declaration renouncing the benefit of s.46 together with the notary's endorsement that he has explained the effect of the renunciation, then in addition to the mortgaged property any other property belonging to the mortgagor becomes liable to be ordered to be sold and to be sold under the decree in an action upon the mortgage, with Civil Procedure Code s.218 applying mutatis mutandis to the seizure and sale of that other property. Section 47A(7)(d) includes the National Savings Bank in the definition of 'lending institution'. Section 47A(2) requires that no process issue against other property until the mortgaged property has been sold and its proceeds applied to the decree, and s.47A(3) makes it the notary's duty to explain the renunciation and its consequences to the mortgagor.
gold_answer_draft.application: The mortgagee is the National Savings Bank, which is a lending institution within Mortgage Act s.47A(7)(d). The principal of the loan is Rs.2,000,000, which exceeds the statutory threshold of one hundred and fifty thousand rupees in s.47A(1). Both gateway conditions are therefore met and the section is available on these facts. Absent the declaration, s.46 would confine the Bank on any decree obtained on the bond to the Rajagiriya land alone, and by s.47 the Bank could not enlarge its remedy by drafting a wider recovery clause into the bond itself. By asking Lihini Manapitiya to sign a separate instrument under s.47A renouncing the benefit of s.46, the Bank secures the right, if the debt is not satisfied, to have her other property ordered sold under the decree in an action upon the mortgage, the seizure and sale being governed mutatis mutandis by Civil Procedure Code s.218. That right is a shortfall remedy rather than a free choice of assets, since s.47A(2) bars process against her other property until the mortgaged land is sold and the proceeds applied. The instrument must be separate, attested by the same notary and witnesses, and carry the notary's endorsement, and under s.47A(3) the notary must explain to her that she is giving up the s.46 protection.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: The Bank requests the declaration in order to escape the restriction in Mortgage Act s.46, which would otherwise limit its recovery on a mortgage decree to the mortgaged Rajagiriya land. Because the National Savings Bank is a lending institution under s.47A(7)(d) and the Rs.2,000,000 principal exceeds the Rs.150,000 threshold, a declaration executed under s.47A(1) renouncing the benefit of s.46 makes Lihini Manapitiya's other property liable to be sold under a decree in an action upon the mortgage, subject to the mortgaged land being sold first under s.47A(2). In short, the Bank wants recourse against her general assets for any shortfall, and s.47A is the only lawful way to obtain it. Whether that recourse is ever exercised depends on facts not given, namely what other property she owns and whether the mortgaged land would realise enough to satisfy the debt.

answer_claims.claim_text: Under Mortgage Act s.46, a decree in a hypothecary action on a mortgage of land, or in an action to recover moneys due on such a mortgage, cannot order any property other than the mortgaged property to be sold, and no other property is liable to be sold in execution of such a decree.
By Mortgage Act s.47 the s.46 restriction has effect notwithstanding anything in any other law or in any mortgage bond or other instrument, so a lender cannot displace it by a term of the bond.

Mortgage Act s.47A(1) allows the benefit of s.46 to be renounced where, at the time of execution of a mortgage bond in favour of a lending institution for a loan whose principal exceeds one hundred and fifty thousand rupees, the mortgagor executes a separate instrument attested by the notary attesting the bond and by the witnesses to it, containing a special declaration of renunciation and the notary's endorsement that he explained its effect.

Where such an instrument is executed, in addition to the mortgaged property any other property belonging to the mortgagor is liable to be ordered to be sold and to be sold under the decree in an action upon the mortgage, and Civil Procedure Code s.218 applies mutatis mutandis to the seizure and sale of that other property.
Mortgage Act s.47A(2) prevents process issuing against the mortgagor's other property until the mortgaged property has been sold and the proceeds applied in satisfaction of the decree.

Mortgage Act s.47A(3) imposes a duty on the notary to explain to the mortgagor that the instrument renounces the benefit of s.46 and that other property becomes liable to be sold in execution of a decree on the mortgage.
The National Savings Bank, the proposed mortgagee, is a lending institution for the purposes of s.47A because s.47A(7)(d) names it expressly.
The principal of the loan, Rs.2,000,000, exceeds the one hundred and fifty thousand rupee threshold in s.47A(1), so the section is available on these facts.
Without the declaration the Bank's recovery under any decree on the bond would be confined to the mortgaged Rajagiriya land, and it could not enlarge that remedy by a clause in the bond.

The Bank requests the s.47A declaration so that, on the mortgagor renouncing the benefit of s.46, her property other than the mortgaged land becomes liable to be sold under a decree in an action upon the mortgage, giving the Bank recourse for any shortfall.
That recourse is a shortfall remedy only: the Bank must first sell the mortgaged land and apply the proceeds before process may issue against her other property.

legal_issues.issue: What interest did Deed of Gift No.1100 of 12 January 2006 vest in Dinesh Gamage, and what was the effect of the death of Sujeewa Jayamini on 21 April 2007 on the life interest she reserved?

On the intestacy of Dinesh Gamage on 23 November 2009, who inherits Lot A and in what proportions, and does Neesha, his daughter by his first marriage, share equally with the three children of the second marriage?
On the intestacy of Neesha Gamage on 20 May 2012, she leaving a husband but no descendants and both her parents having predeceased her, to whom does her share devolve?
On the intestacy of Kasun Gamage on 5 July 2015, he being unmarried and issueless with his father dead and his mother living, to whom does his share devolve?
Which system of personal law governs these intestacies, and is the general law in the Ordinance applicable?

gold_answer_draft.issue: The question is how title to Lot A, allotted to Sujeewa Jayamini by the final decree of 20 October 2001, passed by Deed of Gift No.1100 and then through three successive intestacies (Dinesh Gamage in 2009, Neesha Gamage in 2012 and Kasun Gamage in 2015) to the persons who now own the land and house, and how that chain is set out as a pedigree. A subsidiary issue is whether the general law of intestate succession applies to this family.
gold_answer_draft.rule: Inheritance ab intestato to immovable property in Sri Lanka is governed by Part III of the Matrimonial Rights and Inheritance Ordinance No. 15 of 1876 (s.21), "immovable property" including land and things attached to the earth (s.3), and Part III applying to the estate of anyone dying after the proclamation of the Ordinance (s.20). The Ordinance does not apply to Kandyans, Muslims or Tamils of the Northern Province subject to the Thesawalamai (s.2); nothing in the facts brings any of these persons within those systems, and the analysis proceeds on the general law. A surviving spouse inherits one-half of the estate of the intestate (s.22), and the remaining half devolves in the order descendants, ascendants, collaterals (s.23). Children and remoter descendants are preferent to all others, all children taking equally per capita and the issue of a predeceased child taking per stirpes by representation (s.24). Where descendants fail and only one parent is alive, the surviving parent takes half and the full brothers and sisters, together with the half-brothers and sisters related through the deceased parent and the issue of any of them by representation, take the other half (s.25). Where descendants fail and both parents have failed, the estate goes to the brothers and sisters, whether of the whole or half blood, and their issue by representation (s.26); and where all the half-brothers and sisters are related to the intestate on one side only, they take the whole, unless a grandparent or higher ascendant on the other side is alive (s.29). Persons equally near in degree take per capita and not per stirpes (s.30). A deed transferring an interest in immovable property must be notarially executed to avail in law (Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.2).
gold_answer_draft.application: Sujeewa Jayamini became sole owner of Lot A under the final decree of 20 October 2001. By Deed of Gift No.1100 of 12 January 2006, notarially attested as the Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.2 requires, she gifted Lot A to her son Dinesh Gamage absolutely and irrevocably, reserving a life interest to herself; the gift therefore vested ownership in Dinesh at once, burdened only by that life interest, and her husband Thilak Gamage and her other son Iresh took no interest in Lot A. On her death on 21 April 2007 the reserved life interest came to an end and Dinesh held the entirety free of it. Dinesh died intestate on 23 November 2009 owning the whole of Lot A, which is immovable property within Matrimonial Rights and Inheritance Ordinance s.3, so ss.21 to 30 govern. His widow Lochana took one-half under s.22. Under s.23 and s.24 the other half went to his descendants, who at that date were four children, Neesha (his daughter by his first wife Nimali), Kasun, Kavindu and Piyumi; being equally near in degree they took per capita under s.30, that is one-quarter of the half, or one-eighth of the land, each. Neesha died intestate on 20 May 2012 leaving her husband Rohan Jayaweera but no children. Under s.22 Rohan took one-half of her one-eighth. Her descendants having failed and both her parents having predeceased her (Dinesh on 23 November 2009 and Nimali on 15 July 2010), the other half of her share passed under s.26 to her brothers and sisters. Her only collaterals were Kasun, Kavindu and Piyumi, half-siblings related to her on her father's side alone, so under s.29 they took the whole of that collateral half, per capita under s.30, no grandparent or higher ascendant on the mother's side being disclosed by the facts. Kasun Gamage died on 5 July 2015 unmarried and issueless, holding his original one-eighth together with the share he had taken from Neesha. He left neither spouse nor descendants; his father Dinesh had predeceased him and his mother Lochana survived him. Under s.25 Lochana as the surviving parent took half of his share, and the other half went to his full brother Kavindu and his full sister Piyumi, equally under s.30. Neesha, who would otherwise have been a half-sister on the father's side, had already died in 2012 without issue, so no share fell to her or to anyone representing her.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: The pedigree runs: Sujeewa Jayamini (owner under the final decree of 20 October 2001, married to Thilak Gamage, children Dinesh and Iresh) gifted Lot A by Deed of Gift No.1100 of 12 January 2006 to Dinesh Gamage subject to her life interest, which determined on her death on 21 April 2007, leaving Dinesh sole owner. Dinesh died intestate on 23 November 2009, and Lot A devolved on his widow Lochana and his four children Neesha, Kasun, Kavindu and Piyumi. Neesha died intestate on 20 May 2012 without children, and her interest devolved on her husband Rohan Jayaweera and on her half-siblings Kasun, Kavindu and Piyumi. Kasun died intestate on 5 July 2015 unmarried and issueless, and his interest devolved on his mother Lochana and his full siblings Kavindu and Piyumi. The present owners are therefore Lochana Gamage, Kavindu Gamage, Piyumi Gamage and Rohan Jayaweera. This devolution assumes that the general law of the Ordinance, and not Kandyan law, Muslim law or the Thesawalamai, governs the family, and that no maternal grandparent of Neesha survived her for the purposes of the proviso to s.29.

answer_claims.claim_text: Inheritance ab intestato to immovable property in Sri Lanka is governed by the Matrimonial Rights and Inheritance Ordinance, whatever the deceased person's domicile, and land with a house on it is immovable property for that purpose.

Part III of the Ordinance applies to the estate of any person dying after the proclamation of the Ordinance, but the Ordinance does not apply to Kandyans, Muslims or Tamils of the Northern Province subject to the Thesawalamai.
A surviving spouse inherits one-half of the intestate's property, and the remaining half devolves in the order descendants, ascendants, collaterals.
Children are preferent to all others in the estate of a parent and take equally per capita, the issue of a predeceased child taking by representation; persons equally near in degree take per capita.

Where descendants fail and both parents have failed, the estate goes to the brothers and sisters of the whole or half blood and their issue by representation, and where all the half-siblings are related on one side only they take the whole, subject to a surviving ascendant on the other side.

Where descendants fail and only one parent survives, the surviving parent takes half and the full brothers and sisters, with the half-siblings related through the deceased parent and their issue by representation, take the other half.

Deed of Gift No.1100 of 12 January 2006, being a notarially attested deed, vested ownership of Lot A in Dinesh Gamage subject to the life interest reserved to Sujeewa Jayamini, and that life interest determined on her death on 21 April 2007, leaving Dinesh sole owner.

On the intestacy of Dinesh Gamage on 23 November 2009, Lot A devolved on his widow Lochana as to one-half and on his four children Neesha, Kasun, Kavindu and Piyumi as to the other half in equal per capita shares, his brother Iresh taking nothing.

On the intestacy of Neesha Gamage on 20 May 2012, her husband Rohan Jayaweera took one-half of her share, and because she left no descendants and both her parents had predeceased her, the other half passed to her half-siblings Kasun, Kavindu and Piyumi, who as half-siblings on the father's side alone took the whole of that portion in equal shares.

On the intestacy of Kasun Gamage on 5 July 2015, he leaving no spouse and no issue, his surviving mother Lochana took half of his accumulated share and his full siblings Kavindu and Piyumi took the other half in equal shares, Neesha having already died without issue in 2012.
The present owners of the land and house are Lochana Gamage, Kavindu Gamage, Piyumi Gamage and Rohan Jayaweera.
The pedigree is stated on the assumption that the general law and not Kandyan law, Muslim law or the Thesawalamai governs this family, and that no maternal grandparent of Neesha survived her.

enrichment.original_background: By a final decree dated 20th October 2001 entered in the District Court of Homagama Partition Case No.2026/P land and premises bearing Assessment No.12, Rajamalwatta Road, Panagoda depicted as Lot A in Partition Plan No.2111 dated 23rd May 2001 made by A.L. Jayaweera Licensed Surveyor in extent 20 perches was allotted to Sujeewa Jayamini. She was married to Thilak Gamage and had 2 children namely Dinesh and Iresh. By Deed of Gift No.1100 dated 12th January 2006 attested by Asanka Silva Notary Public, the said Lot A was gifted to her son Dinesh Gamage as an absolute and irrevocable gift subject to life interest of the said Donor Sujeewa Jayamini. Sujeewa Jayamini died on 21 April 2007. Dinesh had a daughter named Neesha by his first wife Nimali. Nimali died on 15th July 2010. Dinesh died intestate on 23rd November 2009 leaving his second wife Lochana and three children namely Kasun, Kavindu and Piyumi. Neesha Gamage married Rohan Jayaweera and died intestate on 20th May 2012 without leaving children. Kasun Gamage died of cancer on 5th July 2015 unmarried and issueless.

legal_issues.issue: What fraction of Lot A does the widow Lochana Gamage presently hold, taking her half of Dinesh's estate together with her share of Kasun's estate?
What fractions do Kavindu Gamage and Piyumi Gamage presently hold, taking their original shares in Dinesh's estate together with their shares of Neesha's and Kasun's estates?
What fraction does Rohan Jayaweera, the widower of Neesha Gamage, presently hold?

gold_answer_draft.issue: The question is what undivided fraction of Lot A, the land and premises at Assessment No.12, Rajamalwatta Road, Panagoda, in extent 20 perches, each surviving heir presently owns after the three intestacies of Dinesh Gamage, Neesha Gamage and Kasun Gamage.
gold_answer_draft.rule: A surviving spouse inherits one-half of the intestate's property (Matrimonial Rights and Inheritance Ordinance s.22) and, subject to that half, the estate devolves first on descendants (s.23). Children take equally per capita (s.24), and persons equally near in degree take per capita and not per stirpes (s.30). Where descendants fail and both parents have failed, the estate goes to brothers and sisters of the whole or half blood and their issue by representation (s.26); where all the half-siblings are related to the intestate on one side only they take the whole, unless an ascendant on the other side survives (s.29). Where descendants fail and only one parent survives, that parent takes half and the full brothers and sisters, together with the half-siblings related through the deceased parent and their issue by representation, take the other half (s.25). The Ordinance governs intestate succession to immovable property in Sri Lanka (s.21, s.3) and does not apply to Kandyans, Muslims or Tamils of the Northern Province subject to the Thesawalamai (s.2).
gold_answer_draft.application: Dinesh Gamage owned the whole of Lot A when he died intestate on 23 November 2009. His widow Lochana took one-half under s.22. The other half went under ss.23, 24 and 30 to his four children then living, Neesha, Kasun, Kavindu and Piyumi, that is one-eighth of the land each. On Neesha's intestacy on 20 May 2012 her one-eighth split under s.22 as to one-half, namely one-sixteenth of the land, to her husband Rohan Jayaweera; the balance one-sixteenth passed under s.26 to her collaterals, who were only her paternal half-siblings, so under s.29 they took that whole one-sixteenth and under s.30 divided it equally, one forty-eighth each to Kasun, Kavindu and Piyumi. Each of the three then held one-eighth plus one forty-eighth, that is seven forty-eighths. Kasun died on 5 July 2015 unmarried and issueless holding seven forty-eighths. His father having predeceased him and his mother surviving, s.25 gave Lochana half of seven forty-eighths, namely seven ninety-sixths, and gave his full siblings Kavindu and Piyumi the other half in equal shares, namely seven one hundred and ninety-seconds each. Lochana therefore holds one-half plus seven ninety-sixths. Kavindu and Piyumi each hold seven forty-eighths plus seven one hundred and ninety-seconds. Rohan Jayaweera holds the one-sixteenth he took in 2012. Expressed over a common denominator of 192, Lochana holds 110/192, Kavindu 35/192, Piyumi 35/192 and Rohan 12/192, which together account for the whole.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: The present shares in Lot A are: Lochana Gamage 55/96 (110/192); Kavindu Gamage 35/192; Piyumi Gamage 35/192; and Rohan Jayaweera 1/16 (12/192). These fractions total unity. They assume that the general law applies to this family rather than Kandyan law, Muslim law or the Thesawalamai, and that no maternal grandparent or higher maternal ascendant of Neesha Gamage was alive on 20 May 2012, since the proviso to s.29 would otherwise halve the portion taken by her paternal half-siblings.

answer_claims.claim_text: A surviving spouse inherits one-half of the intestate's property and the remaining half devolves first on descendants, who take equally per capita when equally near in degree.

Where an intestate leaves no descendants and both parents have failed, the collateral portion goes to brothers and sisters of the whole or half blood, and half-siblings related on one side only take the whole of it subject to a surviving ascendant on the other side.
Where an intestate leaves no descendants and one parent survives, that parent takes half and the full brothers and sisters take the other half.
On the intestacy of Dinesh Gamage in 2009 Lochana took 1/2 of Lot A and Neesha, Kasun, Kavindu and Piyumi took 1/8 each.

On the intestacy of Neesha Gamage in 2012 her husband Rohan Jayaweera took 1/16 of Lot A and her paternal half-siblings Kasun, Kavindu and Piyumi took 1/48 each, so that each of the three then held 7/48.
On the intestacy of Kasun Gamage in 2015 his mother Lochana took 7/96 of Lot A and his full siblings Kavindu and Piyumi took 7/192 each.
Lochana Gamage presently owns 55/96, that is 110/192, of Lot A.
Kavindu Gamage and Piyumi Gamage each presently own 35/192 of Lot A.
Rohan Jayaweera presently owns 1/16, that is 12/192, of Lot A.
The four shares of 110/192, 35/192, 35/192 and 12/192 exhaust the whole of Lot A, and they assume that the general law applies and that no maternal ascendant of Neesha Gamage survived her.

indispensable_provisions.relevant_excerpt: He shall not divulge the secrets confided to him or of which he becomes possessed in the execution of his office, unless with the express permission of his employer or when required to do so by law.
indispensable_provisions.why_relevant: This is the statutory duty of secrecy of a notary. It settles the question directly: a notary may not disclose what he learned in the execution of his office, and the only two gateways to disclosure are the express permission of his employer (here, the testator who instructed and executed the will before him) or a legal requirement to disclose. Whether the notary attested a particular will, and what that will contains, is a secret of exactly this kind.
indispensable_provisions.temporal_note: Rule (1) has stood since the Ordinance came into force in 1907 and is in force at 2020-10. The section as a whole shows amendment events for 2011, 2022 and 2024, but Notaries (Amendment) Act No. 31 of 2022 s.16 and Notaries (Amendment) Act No. 47 of 2011 were read and neither substitutes, amends or repeals rule (1); the 2024 amendment (6-2024 s.3) is in any event after the matter date and so cannot bear on the October 2020 text.

supporting_provisions.relevant_excerpt: Every notary who acts in violation of or disregards or neglects to observe- (a) rules (1), (31) or (32) set out in section 31, shall be guilty of an offence, and shall, on conviction after summary trial before a Magistrate, be liable to a fine not exceeding five thousand rupees, in addition to any civil liability he may incur thereby
supporting_provisions.why_relevant: Shows that breach of the duty of secrecy in rule (1) is not merely a matter of etiquette but a criminal offence, and that criminal liability is in addition to any civil liability. It supports the strength of the advice but is not needed to reach the answer.
supporting_provisions.temporal_note: The corpus text of s.34 is the section substituted by Notaries (Amendment) Act No. 31 of 2022 s.17, which post-dates the matter reference date of 2020-10. A penal provision for breach of the s.31 rules existed before 2022, but its text and the fine then applicable are not in the corpus, so this provision is recorded as supporting only and is not relied on for the conclusion.
supporting_provisions.verifier_note: Excerpt is verbatim, but the corpus text of s.34 is the whole section repealed and substituted by Notaries (Amendment) Act No. 31 of 2022 s.17, so no penalty for breach of rule (1) can be stated from the corpus as at 2020-10; correctly held to supporting only and not relied on for the conclusion.

legal_issues.issue: Whether knowledge that a notary attested a particular will, and knowledge of its contents, is a secret which he became possessed of in the execution of his office.
Who the notary's "employer" is for the purposes of the duty of secrecy where a will was drawn and attested on the testator's instructions, and whether express permission to disclose has been given.
Whether disclosure to the testator's son is "required to do so by law" so as to fall within the second exception.

gold_answer_draft.issue: Whether a notary may confirm to the son of a living testator that he attested the father's will, and tell him what the will contains, when the father has given no permission to disclose and no law requires disclosure.
gold_answer_draft.rule: Notaries Ordinance s.31 rule (1) makes it the duty of every notary not to divulge the secrets confided to him, or of which he becomes possessed in the execution of his office, unless with the express permission of his employer or when required to do so by law. The duty covers everything learned by reason of the office, and the two exceptions are the only gateways to disclosure. Breach of the rule is treated seriously by the Ordinance: it is made a punishable offence, in addition to any civil liability (s.34, the text of which in the corpus is the version substituted in 2022), and gross misconduct in the discharge of the office or repeated breaches of the rules can lead to an inquiry and to suspension or cancellation of the warrant (s.21(1)(b) and (c)).
gold_answer_draft.application: The instructions for the will, the fact that you attested it and the contents of the instrument all came to you in the execution of your notarial office, so they are secrets within rule (1); the protocol you hold is itself a product of that office. Your employer for this purpose is the testator, the father, on whose instructions the will was drawn and executed, not his son. The father is alive, of sound mind, has asked you to keep the matter to yourself and has given no express permission for disclosure, so the first exception is not open. No court or officer has called for the will or its contents, so nothing requires disclosure by law and the second exception is not open either. The son's relationship to the testator does not put him in the place of the employer, and he is neither an executant nor a named executor of the instrument; confirming even that a will exists and that you attested it would divulge part of what the rule protects. If the son wants to know about the will, the proper course is for him to ask his father, or for the father to authorise you expressly.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: No. You should not tell the client about his father's will, and you should not confirm or deny that you attested it. You should decline politely, explain that a notary is bound to keep secret what he learns in the execution of his office, and tell him that you can speak about the will only if his father expressly permits it or if the law requires you to do so.

answer_claims.claim_text: A notary is under a statutory duty not to divulge the secrets confided to him or of which he becomes possessed in the execution of his office.
That duty admits only two exceptions: the express permission of the notary's employer, or a legal requirement to disclose.

Breach of the duty of secrecy exposes the notary to a criminal penalty in addition to civil liability, and gross or repeated breach of the notarial rules can ground an inquiry leading to suspension or cancellation of his warrant.
The fact that you attested the father's will and the contents of that will are secrets you became possessed of in the execution of your office.

The employer whose express permission could release you is the testator, the father on whose instructions the will was drawn and executed, and he is alive, of sound mind and has given no such permission.
Nothing requires you by law to disclose the will or its contents to the son, because no court or officer acting under any written law has called for them.

Being the testator's son does not put the client in the position of the employer, and he is neither an executant nor a named executor of the will, so his relationship gives him no claim on the information.
You should not tell the client about the will, and you should not confirm or deny that you attested it; you may speak about it only if the father expressly permits it or the law requires it.

enrichment.original_background: A client asks whether you have attested his father's will.
enrichment.enriched_background: Ranjith Perera, a businessman of Nugegoda, calls at your office and tells you that he believes his father made a will some years ago. You did in fact draw and attest that will as a notary public on 12 October 2018, and the protocol of it remains in your custody. His father, Sarath Perera, aged 78, is alive, lives on his own and is of sound mind. When he gave you his instructions he asked you to keep the will and its contents to yourself, and he has since neither withdrawn that instruction nor given you permission, in writing or otherwise, to speak about the will to anyone. Ranjith is not an executant of that will and is not named in it as an executor. No court, and no officer acting under any written law, has called on you to produce the will or to disclose what it contains. Ranjith now asks you to confirm whether you attested his father's will and to tell him what it says.

added_facts.fact: You yourself drew and attested the will as a notary public on 12 October 2018 and the protocol remains in your custody.
added_facts.reason: The duty of secrecy bites only on what the notary came to know "in the execution of his office". The original background implies but does not state that the notary acted; making it explicit fixes the source of the knowledge.
added_facts.counterfactual_effect: If the notary had never attested the will and knew nothing of it, there would be no secret acquired in the execution of his office and rule (1) would not engage; he could simply say he has no knowledge of the matter.

added_facts.fact: The father, Sarath Perera, aged 78, is alive and of sound mind.
added_facts.reason: Identifies a living principal who can still give or refuse the express permission that the first exception requires, and keeps the question inside the statute rather than raising the untreated problem of a notary's duty after the testator's death.
added_facts.counterfactual_effect: If the father were dead, the availability of his express permission would fall away and the position of an heir or executor seeking the will would raise questions the corpus does not answer; the question would then be blocked for missing authority rather than answerable on the statute alone.

added_facts.fact: The father instructed you to keep the will and its contents to yourself and has never given you permission, in writing or otherwise, to disclose them to anyone.
added_facts.reason: Closes the first statutory exception, which turns on the express permission of the employer.
added_facts.counterfactual_effect: If the father had expressly authorised you to tell his son about the will, the exception would apply and disclosure within the terms of that permission would be lawful.

added_facts.fact: No court and no officer acting under any written law has required you to produce the will or to disclose its contents.
added_facts.reason: Closes the second statutory exception, which turns on disclosure being required by law.
added_facts.counterfactual_effect: If a court had ordered production of the will or of your protocol, disclosure to that extent would be required by law and the duty of secrecy would yield to it.

added_facts.fact: The client, Ranjith Perera, is the testator's son; he is not an executant of the will and is not named in it as an executor.
added_facts.reason: Fixes the identity of the enquirer and his relationship to the instrument. It does not change the outcome, because the rule looks to the employer's permission rather than to the enquirer's status.
added_facts.counterfactual_effect: Even if the client had been an executant of the will, disclosure would still require the employer's express permission or a legal requirement, so the conclusion would not change on this fact alone.

indispensable_provisions.relevant_excerpt: (25) Where any deed or instrument is executed or acknowledged before more than one notary- (a) the notary who first attests such deed or instrument shall comply with all the requirements of rule (20), and every other notary attesting such deed or instrument shall comply with the requirements of paragraphs (a) to (e) of the aforesaid rule and the provisions of paragraph (g) in respect of erasures, alterations and interpolations made in the signatures attested by him or in his serial number;
indispensable_provisions.why_relevant: This is the provision that expressly permits one deed to be executed or acknowledged before more than one notary and allocates the attestation duties between the notary who attests first and every other attesting notary. It is the direct answer to how two parties who will not meet can execute the same lease, and it fixes the heavier duty on Ruwan Perera as first notary.
indispensable_provisions.temporal_note: Rule (25) has not been touched by Notaries (Amendment) Act No. 47 of 2011, No. 13 of 2013, No. 31 of 2022 or No. 6 of 2024, none of which lists rule (25) among the rules amended. The text was therefore in force at October 2020.

indispensable_provisions.relevant_excerpt: In the case of any deed or instrument which is to be executed by two or more parties, both or all of whom, as the case may be, do not sign the deed or instrument at the same time and place- (i) the deed or instrument shall, for the purposes of the application of rules (6), (7), (23) and (25) set out in section 31, be deemed to be executed or acknowledged at the time when it is first signed by a party, or by two or more parties at the same time and place;
indispensable_provisions.why_relevant: Section 32(2) is the statutory recognition that the parties to one deed may sign at different times and in different places, and it fixes the deemed date of execution for the purposes of rule (25). Without it the split signing in Galle and Colombo would have no statutory footing.
indispensable_provisions.temporal_note: Section 32 carries in_force_from_year 1907 and no amendment events in the corpus, so the text was in force at October 2020.

indispensable_provisions.relevant_excerpt: He shall not authenticate or attest any deed or instrument in any area other than that in which he is authorized to practice, nor in any language other than that in which he is authorized to practice nor authenticate or attest any deed or instrument drawn in any language other than that in which he is authorized to practice.
indispensable_provisions.why_relevant: Rule (22) is why the problem exists at all: Anil Fernando cannot attest in Galle and Ruwan Perera cannot attest in Colombo, so a single notary cannot take both signatures unless one party travels. It makes execution before two notaries the necessary route.
indispensable_provisions.temporal_note: Rule (22) is not among the rules amended by the 2011, 2013, 2022 or 2024 amending Acts and was in force at October 2020. Section 4A (inserted 1976) should be read with it: a warrant to practise in a judicial division is deemed to authorise practice in the judicial zone in which the notary resides.

indispensable_provisions.relevant_excerpt: He shall not authenticate or attest a deed or instrument drawn in Sri Lanka by any other person, unless there shall be endorsed thereon a certificate signed by a notary certifying that such deed or instrument has been drawn by himself.
indispensable_provisions.why_relevant: Ruwan Perera is to draft the lease. Anil Fernando, who will attest the company's signature, is therefore attesting a deed drawn by another person and may do so only if a certificate signed by the notary who drew it is endorsed on the deed.
indispensable_provisions.temporal_note: Rule (2) is not among the rules amended by the 2011, 2013, 2022 or 2024 amending Acts and was in force at October 2020.

indispensable_provisions.relevant_excerpt: He shall not authenticate or attest any deed or instrument unless the person executing the same and the witnesses shall have signed the same in his presence and in the presence of one another, and unless he shall have signed the same in the presence of the executant and of the attesting witnesses.
indispensable_provisions.why_relevant: Rule (12) forbids attestation of a signature not made in the notary's presence. It rules out any arrangement by which one notary attests both parties on the strength of a signature obtained elsewhere, and so requires each party to sign before the notary who attests that party.
indispensable_provisions.temporal_note: Rule (12) is not among the rules amended by the 2011, 2013, 2022 or 2024 amending Acts and was in force at October 2020.

indispensable_provisions.relevant_excerpt: an obligation which, if entered into by a natural person is required by law to be in writing signed by that person and be notarially attested, may be entered into on behalf of the company in writing signed under the name of the company by - (i) two directors of the company; (ii) if there be only one director, by that director; (iii) if the articles of the company so provide, by any other person or class of persons; or (iv) one or more attorneys appointed by the company, and be notarially executed;
indispensable_provisions.why_relevant: Cyril & Cyril (Private) Limited is a body corporate and cannot sign personally. Section 19(1)(a) states how the company signs a notarially attested obligation such as this lease, and it is the provision that lets the company's directors (whom Anil Fernando knows) execute in Colombo.
indispensable_provisions.temporal_note: Section 19 carries in_force_from_year 2007 and no amendment events in the corpus; the Companies (Amendment) Act No. 13 of 2019 in the corpus does not touch it. In force at October 2020.

supporting_provisions.relevant_excerpt: He shall not authenticate or attest any deed or instrument to which at least two witnesses have not subscribed their signatures in letters.
supporting_provisions.why_relevant: Each attestation must be supported by at least two subscribing witnesses, so witnesses must be available at each of the two signings rather than only at the first.
supporting_provisions.temporal_note: Rule (8) is not among the rules amended by the 2011, 2013, 2022 or 2024 amending Acts and was in force at October 2020.

supporting_provisions.relevant_excerpt: no promise, bargain, contract, or agreement for effecting any such object, or for establishing any security, interest, or incumbrance affecting land or other immovable property (other than a lease at will, or for any period not exceeding one month)
supporting_provisions.why_relevant: This is why a notary is needed at all: a lease of immovable property other than a lease at will or for a period not exceeding one month creates an interest in land and is of no force in law unless it is in writing and notarially attested.
supporting_provisions.temporal_note: The corpus text of section 2 is the consolidated text carrying amendment events 60-1947 s.2, 30-2022 s.2 and 4-2024 s.2, so the quoted wording is post-matter-date. supporting_provisions.relevant_excerpt: (b) every notary attesting the deed or instrument shall number such deed or instrument in accordance with the provisions of rule (23); (c) the notary who first attests such deed or instrument shall preserve as his protocol the draft or copy referred to in rule (24), and shall comply with the requirements of that rule, and every other notary attesting such deed or instrument shall supply himself with a certified copy of the deed or instrument, which shall be deemed to be his protocol for the purposes of that rule; and

supporting_provisions.temporal_note: Rule (25) is not among the rules amended by the 2011, 2013, 2022 or 2024 amending Acts and was in force at October 2020.

supporting_provisions.relevant_excerpt: Where any deed or instrument other than a will or codicil shall be executed or acknowledged by two or more parties before more than one notary, the duplicate of such deed or instrument shall be delivered or transmitted by the notary who first attests such deed or instrument to the Registrar of Lands of the district in which he resides; and it shall not be necessary for the other notary or notaries employed in the execution of such deed or instrument to deliver or transmit any duplicate thereof to such registrar.

supporting_provisions.why_relevant: Bears on how the notary in Colombo takes the company's execution and on the material he must keep, and on describing in the attestation an executant whose name differs from his identification document. The quoted text is the current wording.
supporting_provisions.temporal_note: Rule (14) was substituted by Notaries (Amendment) Act No. 31 of 2022 s.16(7) and so was not in force in October 2020; the repealed wording is not recited in the amending Act and is not recoverable from this corpus. supporting_provisions.verifier_note: Excerpt is verbatim but is the rule substituted by Notaries (Amendment) Act No. 31 of 2022 s.16(7); the duty to cause the corporate seal to be affixed and to obtain the signatures of the board is therefore post-date text and must not be used to state how the company executed in October 2020. No claim in fact relies on it and its role is correctly supporting only.

supporting_provisions.relevant_excerpt: He shall not authenticate or attest any deed or instrument unless one of the executants to the deed or instrument or the two attesting witnesses be known to notary or by the identity of the executants to a deed or instrument is established by such notary by inspection of the national identity card, bio-page of the passport or the driving licence of such executants
supporting_provisions.why_relevant: Explains why it matters that Anil Fernando knows the directors but not Russel Perera: a notary may not attest unless the executant before him is known to him or to the attesting witnesses, or is identified from a prescribed document.
supporting_provisions.temporal_note: This is the wording substituted by Notaries (Amendment) Act No. 31 of 2022 s.16(6) and further amended by No. 6 of 2024 s.3(3), so it was not in force in October 2020. The pre-2022 wording survives verbatim in the recital in 31-2022/s16: the notary could not attest unless the person executing the deed was known to him or to at least two of the attesting witnesses. Recorded as supporting only.
supporting_provisions.verifier_note: Excerpt is verbatim but is the post-2022/2024 wording. Unlike rule (20)(b) and (e), the repealed wording of rule (9) is recoverable: Notaries (Amendment) Act No. 31 of 2022 s.16(6) recites it verbatim, and it is added here as PROV-M065-903 so that the identification point in question 1 rests on matter-date text.

supporting_provisions.relevant_excerpt: (i) where any deed or instrument which is to be executed or acknowledged by two or more parties is signed during any month by one or more, as the case may be, of such parties, the notary shall, notwithstanding that the deed or instrument has not been signed by all such-parties, include such deed or instrument in the list required to be delivered or transmitted under paragraph (a)
supporting_provisions.why_relevant: Rule (27) is the rule written for exactly this situation: a deed that two or more parties are to execute but that only one of them has signed. It obliges the notary who took the first signature to list the part-executed deed in his monthly return anyway, to produce the duplicate for inspection if the Registrar of Lands calls for it, and, if the deed is still not signed by all the parties three months after it was first signed, to deliver the duplicate to the registrar, with a right to have it back within two years to complete the deed. It therefore puts a practical limit on the gap between Ruwan Perera taking Russel Perera's signature in Galle and Anil Fernando taking the company's signature in Colombo, which the researcher's map did not record.
supporting_provisions.temporal_note: Rule (27) was in force at October 2020 and was repealed only later, by Notaries (Amendment) Act No. 31 of 2022 s.16(12). The consolidated corpus text of section 31 still carries the rule verbatim, so the October 2020 wording is quotable; that the consolidation retained repealed text is itself a corpus defect and is recorded as a corpus gap.
