legal_issues.issue: Whether one lease agreement may be executed before two different notaries when the parties will not sign at the same time and place.
Whether a notary authorised to practise in Colombo may attest a signature given in Galle, or the reverse.
How a private limited company signs a lease that the law requires to be notarially attested.
What the notary who did not draft the deed must have endorsed on it before he attests it.

gold_answer_draft.issue: Whether, and by what procedure, a lease of a warehouse in Galle can be executed when the corporate party wants its Colombo notary to attest for it, the owner wants his Galle notary to draft and attest, and the owner will not travel to Colombo.
gold_answer_draft.rule: A lease of immovable property other than a lease at will or one not exceeding a month affects an interest in land and must be in writing and notarially attested (Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.2(1)). A notary may not attest a deed in any area other than that in which he is authorised to practise (Notaries Ordinance s.31 rule (22)), and may not attest unless the executant and the witnesses have signed in his presence and in the presence of one another and he has signed in their presence (rule (12)), with at least two witnesses subscribing their signatures in letters (rule (8)). The Ordinance nevertheless allows one deed to be executed or acknowledged before more than one notary: the notary who attests first must comply with all of rule (20), every other attesting notary must comply with paragraphs (a) to (e) of rule (20) and with paragraph (g) as to erasures in the signatures he attests and in his serial number, each notary numbers the deed in his own series under rule (23), the first notary keeps the protocol under rule (24) and every other notary keeps a certified copy as his protocol (s.31 rule (25)). Where the parties do not sign at the same time and place, the deed is deemed executed for the purposes of rules (6), (7), (23) and (25) when it is first signed (s.32(2)(i)). The duplicate goes to the Registrar of Lands of the district in which the first attesting notary resides, and the other notary need not send one (rule (28)). A notary may not attest a deed drawn by another person unless a certificate signed by the notary who drew it is endorsed on the deed (rule (2)). A company enters an obligation that must be notarially attested by signing under the company's name by two directors, or by its sole director, or by a person authorised by its articles, or by an attorney appointed by it, and being notarially executed (Companies Act s.19(1)(a)).
gold_answer_draft.application: Neither notary can take both signatures, because rule (22) confines Anil Fernando to Colombo and Ruwan Perera to Galle, and rule (12) forbids either of them from attesting a signature not made in his presence. Section 31 rule (25) read with section 32(2) removes the difficulty: the lease can be executed in two stages before two notaries. Ruwan Perera drafts the lease in Galle and endorses on it his certificate under rule (2) that he drew it, which is what allows Anil Fernando to attest it later. Russel Perera signs in Galle before Ruwan Perera in the presence of two witnesses who also sign; Ruwan Perera attests there and then as the first notary and, as first notary, must satisfy the whole of rule (20). The deed is then taken to Colombo, where the company signs under its name in the manner permitted by Companies Act s.19(1)(a), before Anil Fernando and two witnesses; Anil Fernando attests as the second notary and needs to comply only with rule (20)(a) to (e) and, as to erasures in the signatures he attested and in his serial number, rule (20)(g). Each notary gives the deed a number in his own consecutive series; Ruwan Perera keeps the protocol and Anil Fernando supplies himself with a certified copy as his protocol. Identification is satisfied on each side by the notary who knows that party, since Ruwan Perera is Russel Perera's own notary and Anil Fernando knows the directors. Because Ruwan Perera attests first and resides in the same district as the warehouse, he transmits the duplicate to the Registrar of Lands of the Galle district under rule (28) and no separate certified copy to another district's registrar arises under rule (29).
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: They can execute the lease as one deed signed at different times and places before two notaries under section 31 rule (25) of the Notaries Ordinance read with section 32(2): Ruwan Perera drafting in Galle, certifying that he drew it, and attesting Russel Perera's signature there as the first notary, and Anil Fernando attesting the company's signature in Colombo as the second notary. Russel Perera therefore does not have to come to Colombo. The order could be reversed, but taking Ruwan Perera first keeps the protocol and the duplicate with the notary who resides in the district where the warehouse lies. This is a proposed statement of the statutory position and is unverified.

answer_claims.claim_text: A lease of immovable property for a period exceeding one month must be in writing and notarially attested to be of force in law.
A notary may not authenticate or attest any deed in an area other than that in which he is authorised to practise.

A notary may not attest a deed unless the executant and the witnesses signed it in his presence and in the presence of one another and he signed it in their presence, and at least two witnesses must subscribe their signatures in letters.

One deed may be executed or acknowledged before more than one notary, the first attesting notary complying with the whole of rule (20) and every other attesting notary with paragraphs (a) to (e) and, as to erasures in the signatures he attested and his serial number, paragraph (g).
Where the parties to a deed do not sign at the same time and place, the deed is deemed executed for the purposes of rules (6), (7), (23) and (25) when it is first signed by a party.

Each attesting notary numbers the deed in his own consecutive series, the first notary preserves the protocol and every other notary supplies himself with a certified copy that is deemed to be his protocol.
A notary may not attest a deed drawn by another person unless a certificate signed by the notary who drew it is endorsed on the deed.

A company enters an obligation that the law requires to be notarially attested by signing under the name of the company by two directors, or by its sole director, or by a person authorised by its articles, or by an attorney appointed by it, and by the deed being notarially executed.
Because Anil Fernando is authorised to practise in Colombo and Ruwan Perera in Galle, neither of them can attest both parties' signatures unless one party travels to the other's area.
Ruwan Perera should draft the lease in Galle and endorse on it his certificate that he drew it, so that Anil Fernando may lawfully attest the same deed in Colombo.

Russel Perera signs in Galle before Ruwan Perera and two witnesses, who sign in his presence and in the presence of one another, and Ruwan Perera attests as the first notary in compliance with the whole of rule (20).

The company then signs the same deed in Colombo under the name of the company in the manner allowed by Companies Act section 19(1)(a), before Anil Fernando and two witnesses, and Anil Fernando attests as the second notary with the lighter duties rule (25)(a) imposes on him.
Ruwan Perera, as the notary who first attests, transmits the duplicate to the Registrar of Lands of the district in which he resides, and Anil Fernando need not transmit one.

The lease can therefore be executed as a single deed signed at different times and places before two notaries, Ruwan Perera attesting in Galle and Anil Fernando attesting in Colombo, so that Russel Perera need not travel to Colombo.

enrichment.original_background: Anil Fernando is a Notary practising in Colombo. A company named Cyril & Cyril (Private) Limited wishes to lease out a warehouse situated in Galle. The company wants Anil Fernando to attest its Lease Agreement. Anil Fernando knows the directors of the said company but he does not know the owner of the warehouse, namely Mr. Russel Perera. Mr.Russel Perera wants his Notary Ruwan Perera who is practising in Galle to draft and attest the Lease Agreement. Russel Perera does not want to come to Colombo.

indispensable_provisions.relevant_excerpt: Inheritance ab interstate to the immovable property in Sri Lanka of a person deceased shall be governed and regulated by the following provisions of this Ordinance wherever such person may have or have had his actual or matrimonial domicile.
indispensable_provisions.why_relevant: Lot B and the undivided one-third share of Lot R are immovable property in Sri Lanka, so devolution on Sunil Peiris's intestacy is governed by this Ordinance rather than by any other system of personal law.
indispensable_provisions.temporal_note: Section stands as originally enacted; the corpus records no amendment event, so the text was in force at the date of death (6 December 2016) and at the matter reference date 2020-04.

indispensable_provisions.relevant_excerpt: When any person shall die intestate as to any of his or her property, leaving a spouse surviving, the surviving spouse shall inherit one-half of the property of such person.
indispensable_provisions.why_relevant: Gives the widow Kusum Peiris one-half of Sunil Peiris's estate, which is the first and largest step in the devolution of Lot B after his death.
indispensable_provisions.temporal_note: Section stands as originally enacted; the corpus records no amendment event, so the text was in force at the date of death (6 December 2016) and at the matter reference date 2020-04.

indispensable_provisions.relevant_excerpt: The children and remoter descendants failing, the inheritance of the deceased goes to his father and mother in case they are both alive; but if only one of the parents be alive, the surviving parent takes half, and the brothers and sisters of the deceased of the full blood, and the issue of any deceased brother or sister of the full blood, by representation, and the brothers and sisters of the half-blood who are related to the intestate by the side of the deceased parent, and the issue of any such deceased brother or sister of the half-blood, by representation, take the other half.
indispensable_provisions.why_relevant: The operative rule. Sunil's father Charles Peiris predeceased him and his mother Pushpa Peiris survived, so Pushpa takes half of the remaining half and the full siblings together with the half-siblings related through the deceased father take the other half. It is also the provision that excludes Keerthi Perera, who is related only through the surviving parent.
indispensable_provisions.temporal_note: Section stands as originally enacted; the corpus records no amendment event, so the text was in force at the date of death (6 December 2016) and at the matter reference date 2020-04.

indispensable_provisions.relevant_excerpt: but if there are only half-brothers and sisters or such issue of one side, the full brothers and sisters and the issue of deceased full brothers and sisters by representation, take then in the first place one-half of the property, and divide the other half with the half-brothers and sisters and their issue by representation.
indispensable_provisions.why_relevant: Governs how the collateral portion is split where the qualifying half-siblings are all on one side. Here only the paternal half-siblings Upul and Wimal qualify, so the full sisters Kanthi and Manel take one-half of the collateral portion first and share the balance with Upul and Wimal.
indispensable_provisions.temporal_note: Section stands as originally enacted; the corpus records no amendment event, so the text was in force at the date of death (6 December 2016) and at the matter reference date 2020-04.
indispensable_provisions.verifier_note: Excerpt and role confirmed against 15-1876/s27; the final limb was applied on the footing that section 25 admits only the paternal half-blood where the mother survives, so within the collateral half there are half-siblings of one side only. An alternative reading that divides the collateral half equally among all four siblings is arguable and would change the fractions; raised for the lawyer, not treated as a defect.

supporting_provisions.relevant_excerpt: Subject to the right of the surviving spouse in the preceding section mentioned, the right of inheritance is divided in the following order as respects (a) descendants, (b) ascendants, (c) collaterals.
supporting_provisions.why_relevant: Sets the order in which the remaining half devolves and confirms that the widow's half is taken off the top before descendants, ascendants and collaterals are considered.

legal_issues.issue: What share the widow Kusum Peiris takes in Lot B and in the undivided one-third share of Lot R.
How the remaining half devolves where the intestate left no descendants, a surviving mother and a predeceased father.
Which half-siblings qualify, and in particular whether Keerthi Perera, related only through the surviving mother, takes anything.
How the collateral portion is divided between the full sisters and the paternal half-brothers.

gold_answer_draft.issue: What share of Lot B, and of the undivided one-third share of the road reservation Lot R, does each surviving heir of Sunil Peiris hold, he having died intestate and childless on 6 December 2016 leaving a widow, a surviving mother, two full sisters, two paternal half-brothers and one maternal half-brother?
gold_answer_draft.rule: Inheritance ab intestato to immovable property in Sri Lanka is governed by the Matrimonial Rights and Inheritance Ordinance (s.21). The surviving spouse inherits one-half of the intestate's property (s.22), and subject to that right inheritance passes in the order descendants, ascendants, collaterals (s.23), descendants being preferent to all others (s.24). Where children and remoter descendants fail and only one parent is alive, the surviving parent takes half and the full brothers and sisters of the deceased, together with the half-brothers and sisters related to the intestate by the side of the deceased parent, take the other half (s.25). Where the qualifying half-siblings are all of one side, the full siblings first take one-half of that portion and divide the remaining half with the half-siblings (s.27), those equally near in degree taking per capita (s.30).
gold_answer_draft.application: Sunil Peiris died intestate on 6 December 2016 leaving no children, so the descendant class fails. His widow Kusum Peiris takes one-half of Lot B and of the undivided one-third share of Lot R under s.22. His father Charles Peiris had predeceased him and his mother Pushpa Peiris was alive, so under s.25 Pushpa takes half of the remaining half, that is one-fourth. The other one-fourth goes to the full sisters Kanthi and Manel, both children of Charles and Pushpa, together with Upul and Wimal, who are half-brothers related to Sunil by the side of the deceased parent Charles. Keerthi Perera is the child of Pushpa by her earlier marriage to Lal Perera and is therefore related to Sunil only through the surviving parent, so s.25 does not admit him. Because the qualifying half-siblings are all on the father's side, s.27 gives Kanthi and Manel one-half of that one-fourth, that is one-eighth or one-sixteenth each, and the remaining one-eighth is divided per capita under s.30 among Kanthi, Manel, Upul and Wimal, that is one thirty-second each.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: The present heirs hold Lot B, and the undivided one-third share of Lot R, as follows: Kusum Peiris, the widow, one-half; Pushpa Peiris, the mother, one-fourth; Kanthi three thirty-seconds; Manel three thirty-seconds; Upul one thirty-second; Wimal one thirty-second. Keerthi Perera takes no share. The six shares exhaust the whole, so all six must join in any conveyance of the entirety of Lot B to the purchaser.

answer_claims.claim_text: Inheritance ab intestato to immovable property in Sri Lanka is governed by the Matrimonial Rights and Inheritance Ordinance, whatever the deceased's domicile.
A surviving spouse inherits one-half of the property of a person dying intestate.
Subject to the surviving spouse's half, inheritance devolves in the order descendants, ascendants, collaterals, descendants being preferent to all others.
Where descendants fail and only one parent survives, the surviving parent takes half and the full siblings together with the half-siblings related through the deceased parent take the other half.
Half-siblings related to the intestate only through the surviving parent are not admitted to the collateral half under section 25.

Where the qualifying half-siblings are all of one side, the full siblings take one-half of the collateral portion in the first place and divide the other half with the half-siblings, those equally near in degree taking per capita.
Sunil Peiris left no children, so the descendant class fails and his widow Kusum Peiris takes one-half of Lot B and of the undivided one-third share of Lot R.
Because Charles Peiris predeceased Sunil and Pushpa Peiris survived him, Pushpa takes one-fourth of the estate as the surviving parent.

Kanthi and Manel are Sunil's full sisters and Upul and Wimal are half-brothers by the side of the deceased father Charles, so those four share the remaining one-fourth, while Keerthi Perera, related only through the surviving mother, is excluded.
Applying section 27 to that one-fourth, Kanthi and Manel take one-eighth between them and the other one-eighth is divided per capita among Kanthi, Manel, Upul and Wimal.

The shares are Kusum Peiris one-half, Pushpa Peiris one-fourth, Kanthi three thirty-seconds, Manel three thirty-seconds, Upul one thirty-second and Wimal one thirty-second, and Keerthi Perera nothing.
All six heirs must join in a conveyance if the purchaser is to obtain the entirety of Lot B and of the undivided one-third share of Lot R.

enrichment.original_background: Anura Perera your client wants to purchase a house and property situated in Rajagiriya said to be belonging to one Kusum Peiris and gives you a copy of a Transfer Deed No. 234 dated 23rd March, 2015 attested by Walter de Silva Notary Public and a copy of a Survey Plan No.1125 dated 2nd January, 2000 made by Anil Silva Licensed Surveyor relating to an allotment of land marked Lot B together with a Reservation for a Road marked Lot R of the Land called Dewatagahawatta in extent of 30 perches situated in Rajagiriya. On examining the documents tendered and after a search at the Colombo Land Registry you observe that Lot B and R depicted in the said Survey Plan are sub-divisions of Lot 1 containing in extent of One Rood and 10 Perches depicted in Partition Plan No. 567 dated 4th April 1998 also made by Anil Silva Licensed Surveyor (herein after referred to as the Original land). 1. The Original Land was allotted to one Alfred Almeida by Final Decree in the District Court of Colombo Partition case No. 1256/P and subsequently by Survey Plan 1125 made by Anil Silva Licensed surveyor sub-divided the said Lot 1 into 4 allotments of land marked A,B,C.and R. and by Deed of Transfer No. 234 dated 23rd March 2015 attested by Walter de Silva Notary Public sold Lot B together with undivided 1/3rd share of the Road Reservation marked Lot R to Sunil Peiris. 2. Sunil Peiris had died Intestate without children on 6th December 2016 leaving behind his widow Kusum Peiris. His estate was duly Administered in District Court Testamentary Case No. 345/16/T and proceedings terminated on 7th May 2018.On examining the Testamentary Case it was observed that the father of Sunil Peiris one Charles Peiris had pre-deceased him leaving behind 2 children named Upul and Wimal by his 1st marriage to Kamala Peiris and three children named Sunil, Kanthi and Manel by his 2nd marriage to Pushpa Peiris. Pushpa Peiris was alive and she too had a child by her 1st marriage to Lal Perera named Keerthi Perera and three children named Sunil, Kanthi and Manel by her 2nd marriage to Charles Peiris.

indispensable_provisions.relevant_excerpt: (12) He shall not authenticate or attest any deed or instrument unless the person executing the same and the witnesses shall have signed the same in his presence and in the presence of one another, and unless he shall have signed the same in the presence of the executant and of the attesting witnesses.
indispensable_provisions.why_relevant: The core rule. A notary may attest only signatures placed before him: the executant and the witnesses must sign in his presence and in the presence of one another, and he must sign in their presence. Nimal Perera therefore cannot attest the bedridden father's signature placed in Kandy before another notary.
indispensable_provisions.temporal_note: Section 31 is held in the corpus as a consolidated text carrying later amendments, but this rule was not touched by Notaries (Amendment) Act No. 31 of 2022 s.16 or No. 6 of 2024 s.3; the wording relied on was in force in April 2020.

indispensable_provisions.relevant_excerpt: (22) He shall not authenticate or attest any deed or instrument in any area other than that in which he is authorized to practice, nor in any language other than that in which he is authorized to practice nor authenticate or attest any deed or instrument drawn in any language other than that in which he is authorized to practice.
indispensable_provisions.why_relevant: Territorial limit on attestation. A notary authorised for Colombo cannot attest in Kandy, so Nimal Perera cannot cure the problem by travelling to the father.
indispensable_provisions.temporal_note: Section 31 is held in the corpus as a consolidated text carrying later amendments, but this rule was not touched by Notaries (Amendment) Act No. 31 of 2022 s.16 or No. 6 of 2024 s.3; the wording relied on was in force in April 2020.

indispensable_provisions.relevant_excerpt: (25) Where any deed or instrument is executed or acknowledged before more than one notary- (a) the notary who first attests such deed or instrument shall comply with all the requirements of rule (20), and every other notary attesting such deed or instrument shall comply with the requirements of paragraphs (a) to (e) of the aforesaid rule and the provisions of paragraph (g) in respect of erasures, alterations and interpolations made in the signatures attested by him or in his serial number;
indispensable_provisions.why_relevant: The Ordinance expressly contemplates one deed executed before more than one notary, and allocates the attestation duties between the notary who first attests and every other attesting notary. This is the mechanism that makes the proposed two-notary execution lawful.
indispensable_provisions.temporal_note: Section 31 is held in the corpus as a consolidated text carrying later amendments, but this rule was not touched by Notaries (Amendment) Act No. 31 of 2022 s.16 or No. 6 of 2024 s.3; the wording relied on was in force in April 2020.

indispensable_provisions.relevant_excerpt: (c) the notary who first attests such deed or instrument shall preserve as his protocol the draft or copy referred to in rule (24), and shall comply with the requirements of that rule, and every other notary attesting such deed or instrument shall supply himself with a certified copy of the deed or instrument, which shall be deemed to be his protocol for the purposes of that rule; and (d) every notary attesting such deed shall, in addition, as far as possible, comply with the other provisions of section 31.
indispensable_provisions.why_relevant: Allocates the protocol: the notary who first attests keeps the protocol under rule (24); the other notary must supply himself with a certified copy which is deemed his protocol. Both must otherwise comply with section 31 as far as possible.
indispensable_provisions.temporal_note: Section 31 is held in the corpus as a consolidated text carrying later amendments, but this rule was not touched by Notaries (Amendment) Act No. 31 of 2022 s.16 or No. 6 of 2024 s.3; the wording relied on was in force in April 2020.

indispensable_provisions.relevant_excerpt: (2) In the case of any deed or instrument which is to be executed by two or more parties, both or all of whom, as the case may be, do not sign the deed or instrument at the same time and place- (i) the deed or instrument shall, for the purposes of the application of rules (6), (7), (23) and (25) set out in section 31, be deemed to be executed or acknowledged at the time when it is first signed by a party, or by two or more parties at the same time and place;
indispensable_provisions.why_relevant: The special-case provision for exactly this fact pattern: parties who do not sign at the same time and place. It fixes the time of execution for rules (6), (7), (23) and (25) at the first signing.
indispensable_provisions.temporal_note: Section unamended since enactment (no amendment events in the corpus); in force at April 2020.

indispensable_provisions.relevant_excerpt: (ii) the deed or instrument shall, for the purposes of the application of rules (18) and (20) set out in section 31, be deemed to be executed or acknowledged whenever it is signed by a party, or by two or more parties at the same time and place; and (iii) the provisions of rule (19) set out in section 31, shall apply after the deed or instrument is first signed by a party, or by two or more parties at the same time and place.
indispensable_provisions.why_relevant: For the date and place rule (18) and the attestation rule (20) the deed is deemed executed on each occasion of signing, so each notary dates and attests his own execution; rule (19), which bars alteration after signature, bites from the first signing.
indispensable_provisions.temporal_note: Section unamended since enactment (no amendment events in the corpus); in force at April 2020.

indispensable_provisions.relevant_excerpt: (20) He shall without delay duly attest every deed or instrument which shall be executed or acknowledged before him, and shall sign and seal such attestation. In such attestation he shall state- (a) that the said deed or instrument was signed by the party and the witnesses thereto in his presence and in the presence of one another;
indispensable_provisions.why_relevant: Each notary must attest without delay, sign and seal, and state that the party and the witnesses signed in his presence and in the presence of one another. Each notary can only certify the execution he actually witnessed.
indispensable_provisions.temporal_note: Section 31 is held in the corpus as a consolidated text carrying later amendments, but this rule was not touched by Notaries (Amendment) Act No. 31 of 2022 s.16 or No. 6 of 2024 s.3; the wording relied on was in force in April 2020.

supporting_provisions.relevant_excerpt: (b) every notary attesting the deed or instrument shall number such deed or instrument in accordance with the provisions of rule (23);
supporting_provisions.why_relevant: Each attesting notary must give the deed a number in his own consecutive series, so the deed will bear two numbers, one from the Colombo notary and one from the Kandy notary.
supporting_provisions.temporal_note: Section 31 is held in the corpus as a consolidated text carrying later amendments, but this rule was not touched by Notaries (Amendment) Act No. 31 of 2022 s.16 or No. 6 of 2024 s.3; the wording relied on was in force in April 2020.

supporting_provisions.relevant_excerpt: (28) Where any deed or instrument other than a will or codicil shall be executed or acknowledged by two or more parties before more than one notary, the duplicate of such deed or instrument shall be delivered or transmitted by the notary who first attests such deed or instrument to the Registrar of Lands of the district in which he resides; and it shall not be necessary for the other notary or notaries employed in the execution of such deed or instrument to deliver or transmit any duplicate thereof to such registrar.

legal_issues.issue: Whether a Colombo notary may attest a partition deed in respect of a signature placed in Kandy before a different notary, given the requirement that the executant and witnesses sign in the attesting notary's presence.

Whether the Notaries Ordinance permits one deed to be executed before two notaries at different times and places, and how the attestation, dating, numbering, protocol and duplicate duties are then divided.
Whether the Colombo notary could instead travel to Kandy and attest the bedridden father's execution there.

gold_answer_draft.issue: What does the Notaries Ordinance require where one partition deed is to be signed by a bedridden executant in Kandy before a Kandy notary and by his two brothers in Colombo before Nimal Perera, and may Nimal Perera attest the whole deed?
gold_answer_draft.rule: Notaries Ordinance rule 31(12) forbids a notary to authenticate or attest any deed unless the person executing it and the witnesses signed it in his presence and in the presence of one another and he signed it in their presence, so a notary can attest only the execution that took place before him; rule 31(8) requires at least two witnesses to subscribe their signatures in letters. Rule 31(22), read with s.9 and s.4A, forbids a notary to attest in any area other than the area in which he is authorised to practise. Rule 31(25) expressly allows one deed to be executed or acknowledged before more than one notary: under 31(25)(a) the notary who first attests must comply with the whole of rule 31(20) and every other attesting notary with paragraphs (a) to (e) of that rule and with paragraph (g) for erasures in the signatures he attested; under 31(25)(b), read with rule 31(23), each notary numbers the deed in his own consecutive series; under 31(25)(c) the first attesting notary preserves the protocol required by rule 31(24) and the other notary supplies himself with a certified copy which is deemed his protocol; and under 31(25)(d) every attesting notary must, as far as possible, comply with the other provisions of s.31. Section 32(2) governs a deed executed by two or more parties who do not sign at the same time and place: for rules (6), (7), (23) and (25) it is deemed executed when first signed, and for rules (18) and (20) it is deemed executed whenever it is signed, while rule (19), which forbids erasure, alteration or interpolation after signature, applies from the first signing. Rule 31(18) requires each notary to insert in letters the day, month, year and place of the execution before him, and rule 31(20)(a) and (c) require each attestation to state that the party and witnesses signed in his presence and in the presence of one another and to give the date, the place and the attesting witnesses. Rule 31(28) puts the duty to transmit the duplicate to the Registrar of Lands on the notary who first attests and relieves the other notary of it; rule 31(29) adds a certified copy to the Registrar of Lands of the district where the land lies if that is a different district. Rule 31(26)(c) requires a part-executed deed to be included in the monthly list and allows the Registrar of Lands to call for the duplicate, and if the deed is not signed by all parties within three months of the first signature the notary may be required to deliver the duplicate to the registrar. Section 33 saves an instrument from invalidity for a failure in a matter of form only, and s.34(1)(c) makes breach of a s.31 rule an offence triable summarily, in addition to civil liability.
gold_answer_draft.application: The father cannot come to Colombo and the brothers will sign before Nimal Perera in Colombo, so the three executants will not sign at the same time and place. Rule 31(12) means Nimal Perera cannot attest the father's signature, which will be made in Kandy before another notary and outside his sight, and he cannot sign the attestation in the father's presence. He also cannot travel to Kandy and attest there, because rule 31(22) confines him to the area in which he is authorised to practise, and s.9 and s.4A tie that area to his warrant and to the judicial zone in which he resides. The lawful course is the one the facts already suggest: the Kandy notary attests the father's execution in Kandy, with two witnesses who sign in that notary's presence and in the presence of one another, and Nimal Perera attests the two brothers' execution in Colombo with two witnesses signing before him. Rule 31(25) then divides the duties. Whichever of the two attests first must comply with the whole of rule 31(20), keep the protocol under rules 31(24) and 31(25)(c) and transmit the duplicate under rule 31(28); the other confines his attestation to paragraphs (a) to (e) of rule 31(20) and keeps a certified copy as his protocol. Each numbers the deed in his own series under rules 31(23) and 31(25)(b), and each states the true date and place of the execution before him under rules 31(18) and 31(20)(c). Section 32(2) makes the two dates workable: the deed counts as executed at the first signing for numbering and for the multi-notary rule, and as executed on each occasion for the dating and attestation rules, and nothing may be altered after the first signature. Because the executions may fall in different months, rule 31(26)(c) requires the part-executed deed to be listed, and the execution should be completed within three months of the first signature. The facts do not say where the land subject to the partition lies or which notary will attest first, so rule 31(29) and the allocation of the first-attesting notary's duties can only be stated conditionally.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: Nimal Perera may not attest the whole partition deed, and may not go to Kandy to attest the father's execution. Under the Notaries Ordinance the deed may lawfully be executed before two notaries: the Kandy notary attesting the bedridden father's execution in Kandy and Nimal Perera attesting the two brothers' execution in Colombo, each with two witnesses signing in his presence, each dating and numbering his own execution and each attesting only what he witnessed, with the notary who attests first holding the protocol and transmitting the duplicate under rules 31(25), 31(24) and 31(28), and s.32(2) supplying the timing rules. If Nimal Perera instead attested the father's signature he would breach rule 31(12) and commit an offence under s.34.

answer_claims.claim_text: A notary may not authenticate or attest a deed unless the executant and the witnesses signed it in his presence and in the presence of one another and he signed it in their presence.
At least two witnesses must subscribe their signatures in letters to a deed the notary attests.
A notary may not attest a deed in any area other than the area in which he is authorised to practise, that area being fixed by his warrant and extending to the judicial zone in which he resides.
The Ordinance permits one deed to be executed or acknowledged before more than one notary, and allocates the attestation duties between the notary who first attests and every other attesting notary.

Each attesting notary numbers the deed in his own consecutive series, the first attesting notary keeps the protocol and the other notary supplies himself with a certified copy which is deemed his protocol, and every attesting notary must otherwise comply with section 31 as far as possible.

Where two or more parties do not sign at the same time and place, the deed is deemed executed at the first signing for rules (6), (7), (23) and (25), is deemed executed on each occasion of signing for rules (18) and (20), and the bar on erasure, alteration or interpolation applies from the first signing.

Each notary must insert in letters the day, month and year and the place of the execution before him, and must state in his attestation that the party and the witnesses signed in his presence and in the presence of one another, together with the date, the place and the attesting witnesses.

Where a deed is executed by two or more parties before more than one notary the duplicate is transmitted to the Registrar of Lands by the notary who first attests it and the other notary need not transmit one, and a certified copy must also go to the Registrar of Lands of the district in which the land lies if that is a different district.

A deed signed by only some of the parties must still be included in the notary's monthly list and produced if the Registrar of Lands calls for it, and if all parties have not signed within three months of the first signature the notary may be required to deliver the duplicate to the registrar.
Nimal Perera cannot attest the bedridden father's signature, because that signature will be placed in Kandy before another notary and not in Nimal Perera's presence.
Nimal Perera cannot cure this by travelling to Kandy himself, because he practises in Colombo and may not attest outside the area in which he is authorised to practise.

The deed may be attested by the Kandy notary as to the father's execution in Kandy and by Nimal Perera as to the two brothers' execution in Colombo, each with two witnesses signing in the presence of the attesting notary and of one another.

Because the three executants will sign at different times and places, each notary dates and attests only the execution before him, each numbers the deed in his own series, the notary attesting first keeps the protocol and transmits the duplicate, and nothing may be altered after the first signature.
The execution should be completed within three months of the first signature, failing which the notary who holds the duplicate may be called on to deliver it to the Registrar of Lands.

The facts do not state where the partitioned land lies or which notary will attest first, so the destination of the certified copy and the allocation of the first-attesting notary's duties can only be stated conditionally.

Nimal Perera may not attest the whole partition deed and may not attest in Kandy; the deed may lawfully be executed before the two notaries, each attesting only the execution that took place before him.

If Nimal Perera attested the father's signature without the father having signed before him he would breach rule 31(12) and commit an offence punishable on summary trial in addition to any civil liability, and section 33 would not save the position because the breach is not a matter of form.

enrichment.original_background: Nimal Perera is a Notary practicing in Colombo. Waruna Liyanage a client of his said that his father who is very sick and bed ridden living in Kandy wishes to execute a Partition Deed by himself together with his two brothers and wanted Nimal Perera to attest it. A Notary in Kandy is willing to visit the bed ridden father and get it executed by him. The other two brothers are willing to come to Colombo to execute it before Nimal Perera.

legal_issues.issue: Whether the Indenture of Lease granted to Jayantha de Siva and the mortgage bond in favour of the Lending Institution are instruments affecting the Nugegoda land, so that their ranking is governed by the Registration of Documents Ordinance.
Whether the mortgage bond, executed after the lease, can nevertheless take priority over the lease, and on what condition.

What Kamal Perera and the Lending Institution must do in the land registry to obtain and protect that priority, and what Kamal can lawfully promise the Lending Institution if the lease has already been registered.

gold_answer_draft.issue: Kamal has already leased the Nugegoda house to Jayantha de Siva by an Indenture of Lease and has since mortgaged the same house to a Lending Institution, which wants its Mortgage Bond to rank ahead of the lease. The question is whether the later mortgage bond can take priority over the earlier lease, and what Kamal and the lender must do to achieve it.
gold_answer_draft.rule: Priority between competing instruments affecting the same land is decided by the land register and not by the order of execution. Under Registration of Documents Ordinance s.8(b) every instrument that creates, charges or encumbers any interest in land is an instrument affecting land, which covers both an Indenture of Lease and a mortgage bond; only a tenancy at will, a tenancy for a month or less, or one determinable on a month's notice is excluded by proviso (xi) to s.8. Section 7(1) then provides that such an instrument, unless duly registered, is void as against a party claiming an adverse interest on valuable consideration under a subsequent instrument which is duly registered. Section 14(2) provides that an instrument is not duly registered unless it is registered in the proper book and folio for the land, and s.27(1) provides that for the purpose of priority the time of presentation in the day book is taken as the time of registration. Section 30(2) allows an intending mortgagee to register a priority notice before the bond is executed, in which case the bond, if registered while the notice is in force, is deemed registered at the time of the notice, and s.30(3) blocks registration of any competing instrument executed by the owner while a notice registered with his written consent is in force. Section 7(2) preserves an exception where the prior registration was obtained by fraud or collusion, and s.7(4) makes clear that registration confers nothing beyond that priority. Under Notaries Ordinance s.31 rule (17)(a) the notary must search the land registry before drawing the bond.
gold_answer_draft.application: The Indenture of Lease creates an interest in the Nugegoda house in favour of Jayantha de Siva and the Mortgage Bond charges the same house, so both fall within s.8(b), provided the lease is for more than a month. The loan is valuable consideration, so the Lending Institution is a party claiming an adverse interest on valuable consideration within s.7(1). Everything therefore turns on the state of the folio for this land, which the notary must ascertain by a search under s.31 rule (17)(a) of the Notaries Ordinance. If the Indenture of Lease has not been registered, the Mortgage Bond, once duly registered in the correct folio under s.14(2), will under s.7(1) render the lease void as against the Lending Institution and the bond will rank first, priority running from the time of presentation under s.27(1). To make that outcome secure against anything Kamal might do in the meantime, the Lending Institution should register a priority notice under s.30 before the bond is executed, so that the bond is deemed registered from the date of the notice and no competing instrument executed by Kamal can be registered while the notice is in force. If, on the other hand, the lease has already been registered, s.7(1) gives Kamal nothing to work with: the lease is duly registered and prior, the later bond cannot displace it, and Kamal cannot honestly promise the Lending Institution first place. Kamal must also be warned that under s.7(2) fraud or collusion in securing the prior registration would defeat the priority so obtained, so concealing the lease from the lender or from the registry is not an option, and that under s.7(4) registration of the bond secures priority and nothing else. The facts do not state the term of the lease, whether the lease has been registered, or whether the bond has yet been executed, so the advice has to be given on both footings.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: Advise Kamal that priority here is a question of registration, not of the dates of the deeds. A search of the folio for the Nugegoda land must be done first. If the Indenture of Lease is unregistered, the Lending Institution can obtain the priority it wants by registering a priority notice under Registration of Documents Ordinance s.30 and then having the Mortgage Bond duly registered in the proper folio while that notice is in force, whereupon the lease is void against the bond under s.7(1). If the lease is already registered, the Mortgage Bond cannot be given priority over it by registration, and Kamal should tell the Lending Institution so and take the matter up with the lessee rather than conceal the lease, since fraud or collusion would in any event defeat the priority under s.7(2).

answer_claims.claim_text: An Indenture of Lease and a mortgage bond are both instruments affecting land, because Registration of Documents Ordinance s.8(b) covers every instrument which purports or operates to create, charge or encumber any interest in land.
A lease at will, for a period not exceeding one month, or determinable by the landlord on not more than a month's notice, is outside the registration scheme by virtue of proviso (xi) to s.8.

Under Registration of Documents Ordinance s.7(1) an instrument that is not duly registered is void as against a party claiming an adverse interest on valuable consideration under a subsequent instrument which is duly registered.

An instrument is not duly registered unless it is entered in the book and folio required by s.14, and for the purpose of priority the time of presentation in the day book is taken as the time of registration under s.27(1).

An intending mortgagee may register a priority notice under s.30, and an instrument registered while that notice is in force is deemed to have been registered at the time of registration of the notice.

Registration of the Mortgage Bond confers priority and nothing more; it cures no defect in the instrument, and under s.7(2) fraud or collusion in securing the prior registration defeats the priority so obtained.

The notary drawing the Mortgage Bond must search the registers of the land registry to ascertain the state of the title and whether any prior deed affecting the Nugegoda land has been registered, which is how the position of the Indenture of Lease is established.

The loan advanced by the Lending Institution is valuable consideration, so the Lending Institution is a party claiming an adverse interest on valuable consideration under a subsequent instrument for the purposes of s.7(1).
If the Indenture of Lease has not been registered, the Mortgage Bond duly registered in the proper folio will render the lease void as against the Lending Institution and will rank ahead of it.

The Lending Institution should register a priority notice before the Mortgage Bond is executed, so that the bond is deemed registered from the date of the notice and no instrument executed by Kamal Perera can be registered against the land while the notice is in force.

If the Indenture of Lease has already been duly registered, the later Mortgage Bond cannot be given priority over it by registration, because s.7(1) protects only the party whose registered instrument is subsequent to an unregistered one.

Kamal Perera should be advised that priority turns on the state of the register, that a search must be made first, that if the lease is unregistered the Lending Institution can obtain priority through a priority notice followed by due registration of the Mortgage Bond, and that if the lease is registered he cannot promise the lender first place and must not conceal the lease.

legal_issues.issue: Who is liable to pay the stamp duty on the Mortgage Bond, and whether that liability can be displaced by agreement between Kamal Perera and the Lending Institution.
To whom the duty on a mortgage bond over immovable property is paid, given that the house is in the Western Province.
What the procedure is: when the duty must be paid, how payment is evidenced on the instrument, what the notary must do before attesting, and what follows if the bond is insufficiently stamped.

gold_answer_draft.issue: Who must pay the stamp duty on the Mortgage Bond securing Rs.3,000,000 over the Nugegoda house, to whom it is paid, and by what procedure.
gold_answer_draft.rule: Stamp Duty (Special Provisions) Act, No. 12 of 2006 s.4(g) makes a bond or mortgage for a definite and certain sum affecting property a specified instrument, and s.3(1) charges duty on it. Section 6 provides that, otherwise than in cases where there is an agreement to the contrary, stamp duty is payable by the persons it lists, and since no paragraph of s.6 names a bond or mortgage, paragraph (e) applies and the duty falls on the person drawing, making or executing the instrument. Section 8(1) requires the duty to be paid by affixing adhesive stamps to the required value prior to or at the time of execution, with the value specified on the face of the instrument. Section 8(2) provides that duty on a specified instrument relating to a mortgage or lease of immovable property may instead be paid to a prescribed bank prior to or at the time of execution, or, where that is impossible for reasons beyond the control of the person liable, within seven days from execution, and that the bank issues a certificate in the prescribed form which is affixed to the instrument. Section 8(3) requires the executant to cancel adhesive stamps at execution by writing his name or initials across each stamp and to perforate any stamp of fifty rupees or more, and s.8(4) deems an instrument bearing uncancelled stamps unstamped to that extent. Section 2 charges the Commissioner-General with the implementation and administration of the Act, and s.10 empowers an Assessor to assess the duty on the person liable and serve a notice to pay where an instrument is not duly stamped. Section 9 sends duty to a Provincial Council only where the instrument is one referred to in List I of the Ninth Schedule to the Constitution, and Western Province Financial Statute, No. 6 of 1990 s.37 charges provincial duty on transfers of immovable property, court documents and motor vehicle transfers alone. Under Notaries Ordinance s.31 rule (6) a notary must not attest a deed or instrument unless he has an assurance that the required stamp duty is provided.
gold_answer_draft.application: The Mortgage Bond is a specified instrument under s.4(g). No paragraph of s.6 deals with a bond or mortgage, so paragraph (e) governs and the duty is payable by the person drawing, making or executing the bond, that is Kamal Perera as mortgagor. That allocation is expressly subject to any agreement to the contrary in the opening words of s.6, so if the bond or the loan agreement with the Lending Institution provides otherwise, that agreement prevails; a lending institution's bond ordinarily puts the duty on the borrower, which leaves it with Kamal in any event. Because the bond relates to a mortgage of immovable property, s.8(2) applies and the duty may be paid to a prescribed bank before or at execution, with the bank's certificate of payment in the prescribed form affixed to the instrument; if payment cannot be made by then for reasons beyond Kamal's control it must be made to the prescribed bank within seven days of execution. If adhesive stamps are used instead under s.8(1) they must be affixed to the required value before or at execution, the value must be specified on the face of the bond, Kamal must cancel them at execution under s.8(3) and perforate any stamp of fifty rupees or more, failing which the bond is treated as unstamped to that extent under s.8(4). The house is in Nugegoda, so s.9 and the Western Province Financial Statute have to be considered, but s.37 of that statute does not charge mortgage bonds, so the duty is not a Provincial Council receipt; it is national duty administered by the Commissioner-General under s.2. The notary attesting the bond must not do so unless satisfied under Notaries Ordinance s.31 rule (6) that the required stamp duty is provided. If the bond turns out to be insufficiently stamped, an Assessor may under s.10 assess the duty payable by the person liable and serve a notice requiring payment within the time stated.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: Kamal Perera, as the person drawing, making and executing the Mortgage Bond, is the person liable for the stamp duty under Stamp Duty (Special Provisions) Act s.6(e), unless the bond or the loan agreement provides otherwise. The duty is not payable to the Western Provincial Council, because Western Province Financial Statute s.37 does not charge mortgage bonds; it is payable under the national Act, which the Commissioner-General administers. As to procedure, the duty must be met prior to or at the time of execution, either by affixing and cancelling adhesive stamps of the required value with the value stated on the face of the bond, or, as is usual for a mortgage of immovable property, by payment to a prescribed bank whose certificate in the prescribed form is affixed to the bond, with the seven day fallback in s.8(2) where payment beforehand was impossible for reasons beyond his control. The notary will not attest the bond without an assurance that the duty is provided, and an understamped bond exposes Kamal to an assessment and a notice to pay from an Assessor.

answer_claims.claim_text: A bond or mortgage for a definite and certain sum of money affecting any property is a specified instrument chargeable with stamp duty under Stamp Duty (Special Provisions) Act s.4(g) read with s.3(1).

Section 6 allocates liability for stamp duty otherwise than in cases where there is an agreement to the contrary, so any agreement between the parties on who bears the duty displaces the statutory allocation.
No paragraph of s.6 names a bond or mortgage, so the residual limb in paragraph (e) applies and the duty is payable by the person drawing, making or executing the instrument.
Under s.8(1) the duty must be paid by affixing adhesive stamps to the required value prior to or at the time of execution, and the value paid must be specified on the face of the instrument.

Under s.8(2) duty on an instrument relating to a mortgage of immovable property may be paid to a prescribed bank prior to or at execution, or within seven days of execution where payment by then was impossible for reasons beyond the control of the person liable, and the bank's certificate in the prescribed form is affixed to the instrument.

Adhesive stamps must be cancelled by the executant at the time of execution by writing his name or initials across each stamp, stamps of fifty rupees or more must also be perforated, and stamps not so cancelled leave the instrument unstamped to the extent of their value.

The Act is implemented and administered by the Commissioner-General, and an Assessor who finds an instrument not duly stamped may assess the duty on the person liable and serve a notice requiring payment within a stated time.
A notary must not attest a deed or instrument unless he has an assurance that the required stamp duty is provided.

Kamal Perera is the person drawing, making and executing the Mortgage Bond as mortgagor, so the duty falls on him under s.6(e) unless the bond or the loan arrangement with the Lending Institution provides otherwise.

Although the house is at Nugegoda in the Western Province, Western Province Financial Statute s.37 charges provincial stamp duty only on transfers of immovable property, court documents and motor vehicle transfers, so the duty on this Mortgage Bond is not paid to the Western Provincial Council under s.9 of the 2006 Act.

Because the Mortgage Bond relates to a mortgage of immovable property, the practical route is payment to a prescribed bank before or at execution, with the bank certificate affixed to the bond, rather than adhesive stamps.

Kamal Perera must pay the stamp duty on the Mortgage Bond unless the bond provides otherwise; it is payable under the national Act administered by the Commissioner-General and not to the Western Provincial Council; and it must be paid to a prescribed bank, or by affixing and cancelling adhesive stamps, prior to or at the time of execution, with the seven day fallback in s.8(2), the notary declining to attest until the duty is provided.

legal_issues.issue: Which law governs intestate succession to Lot 5B, being immovable property in Sri Lanka left by Lalith Perera on his death on 2 March 2018?
What shares did Kamani, Hasini and Kushan take in Lot 5B on that intestacy?
What is the effect of Kamani's gift of her share to her three children, including Ruvini, who is her daughter by an earlier marriage and not an heir of Lalith Perera?

gold_answer_draft.issue: What fractions of premises Assessment No. 3/2B, being Lot 5B in Plan No. 225, are presently held by each of the persons who take through Lalith Perera, who died intestate on 2 March 2018 leaving his wife Kamani and his children Hasini and Kushan, Kamani having afterwards gifted her share to her three children including Ruvini, her daughter by an earlier marriage?
gold_answer_draft.rule: Inheritance ab intestato to immovable property in Sri Lanka is governed by Part III of the Matrimonial Rights and Inheritance Ordinance No. 15 of 1876 (s.21), which applies to the estate of a person who dies after the proclamation of the Ordinance and who, if married, married after it (s.20). A surviving spouse inherits one-half of the intestate's property (s.22). Subject to that half, descendants are preferent to all others and all the children take equally per capita (ss.23 and 24). A woman governed by the Thesawalamai needs her husband's written consent only for a disposition made during the marriage (Jaffna Matrimonial Rights and Inheritance Ordinance No. 1 of 1911 s.6), and on the death of a spouse only the deceased spouse's thediatheddam is divided, the survivor's own acquisition remaining hers (s.20).
gold_answer_draft.application: Mala Nadaraja bought Lot 5B for value on 1 August 2014 from Malika Peiris, who was then 20 years old, so that link is unaffected by the minority that spoils the Lot 5A branch. Lot 5B was Mala Nadaraja's own acquisition and none of it devolved on Mohan Nadaraja's heirs at his death, and when she executed Deed of Transfer No. 789 on 5 April 2017 she was a widow, so no written consent was required and Lalith Perera took the whole of Lot 5B. On his intestate death on 2 March 2018, Kamani as surviving spouse took one-half, and the remaining one-half went to Hasini and Kushan in equal shares, one-fourth each. Ruvini is Kamani's daughter by an earlier marriage and not a descendant of Lalith Perera, so she inherited nothing from him. Kamani then gifted her one-half to Hasini, Kushan and Ruvini, giving each of them a further one-sixth. Hasini's total is one-fourth plus one-sixth, that is five-twelfths, and Kushan's is the same; Ruvini holds one-sixth, or two-twelfths; and Kamani, having given away her whole half, retains nothing.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: Premises Assessment No. 3/2B is presently owned as to five-twelfths by Hasini, five-twelfths by Kushan and one-sixth, that is two-twelfths, by Ruvini. Kamani retains no share. Ruvini's interest comes wholly from Kamani's gift and not from any right of inheritance in the estate of Lalith Perera.

A surviving spouse inherits one-half of the property of a person who dies intestate.
Subject to the surviving spouse's half, the children are preferent to all others and take equally per capita.
Mala Nadaraja needed no consent for Deed of Transfer No. 789 of 5 April 2017 because her husband was already dead, and Lot 5B was her own thediatheddam, none of which had devolved on his heirs.

indispensable_provisions.formal_title: Revocation of Irrevocable Deeds of Gift on the Ground of Gross Ingratitude Act

indispensable_provisions.why_relevant: Directly answers the question. indispensable_provisions.why_relevant: A necessary statutory condition on the remedy in section 2. Whether the gift can in fact still be revoked depends on both limbs of this time bar being satisfied, so the answer turns on the deed date and on the date the cause of action arose.

legal_issues.issue: Whether a recital in a deed of gift that the gift is absolute and irrevocable prevents the gift from being revoked at all.
If revocation is possible, on what ground, at whose instance and by what mode it may be effected, and whether the donor can revoke by his own act.
Whether the revocation action is open in time, measured both from the execution of the deed and from the date the cause of action arose.
What must accompany the plaint in such an action and what procedure governs it.

gold_answer_draft.issue: Whether a deed of gift which on its face declares the gift to be absolute and irrevocable can nevertheless be revoked; and if it can, on what ground, at whose instance, by what mode, within what time and with what procedural steps.
gold_answer_draft.rule: A statement in the deed that the gift is absolute and irrevocable prevents the donor from undoing the gift by his own act, but it does not put the gift beyond recall. Under the Revocation of Irrevocable Deeds of Gift on the Ground of Gross Ingratitude Act, No. 5 of 2017, s.2, an irrevocable deed of gift may be revoked on the ground of gross ingratitude, and only on an order made by a competent court in an action filed by the donor against the donee. Section 2 is exhaustive both as to the ground and as to the mode, so a unilateral deed of revocation by the donor will not do. Section 3 bars the court from entertaining such an action unless it is filed within ten years from the date of execution of the deed of gift and within two years from the date on which the cause of action arose; both limbs must be met. Section 4(1) requires the plaintiff to file with the plaint an application for registration of the action as a lis pendens, addressed to the Registrar of Lands of the district in which the deed sought to be revoked is registered or, where it is unregistered, of the district in which the land lies; Registrar of Lands is defined in s.6 by reference to the Registration of Documents Ordinance (Chapter 117), and s.11(6) of that Ordinance treats a duly registered action as pending from the time of registration. Section 5 applies the Civil Procedure Code to the action. The 2017 Act does not define gross ingratitude, so whether proved conduct reaches that standard is for the court on the evidence.
gold_answer_draft.application: The deed of 12 March 2018 recites that the gift is absolute and irrevocable, so Wimalasena cannot simply execute an instrument cancelling it, and the donee refuses to join in any cancellation. His only route is an action under s.2 against Chandana. The conduct relied on, withholding food and medicine from an elderly donor, an assault, and finally locking him out of the very house that was gifted, is pleaded as gross ingratitude; whether it is held to amount to gross ingratitude is a matter for the court, because the Act sets no definition. On the time bar in s.3, an action filed in or shortly after October 2019 is about one year and seven months after execution of the deed on 12 March 2018, well inside ten years, and about five months after the cause of action arose on 20 May 2019, well inside two years, so both limbs are satisfied. Because the deed was registered in the Gampaha land registry, the application for registration of lis pendens under s.4(1)(a) is addressed to the Registrar of Lands of the Gampaha district, in triplicate and substantially in the form set out in the Registration of Documents Ordinance, and it must be filed in court with the plaint; registration is what protects the donor if Chandana attempts to dispose of the land while the action is pending. The action then proceeds under the Civil Procedure Code by virtue of s.5.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: Yes, the gift can be revoked, but not by the donor's own act and not on any ground he chooses. Notwithstanding the recital that it is absolute and irrevocable, the deed may be revoked only by an order of a competent court, on the single ground of gross ingratitude, in an action filed by the donor against the donee under s.2 of Act No. 5 of 2017. On these facts the action is within both limbs of the s.3 time bar, must be filed with a lis pendens application under s.4 addressed to the Registrar of Lands, Gampaha, and is prosecuted under the Civil Procedure Code under s.5. Whether relief is in fact granted depends on the court accepting that the donee's proved conduct amounts to gross ingratitude, a question the Act leaves open.

answer_claims.claim_text: A recital that a deed of gift is absolute and irrevocable does not make the gift incapable of being revoked; the statute expressly contemplates revocation of an irrevocable deed of gift.
The only statutory ground on which an irrevocable deed of gift may be revoked is gross ingratitude.
Revocation can be effected only by an order of a competent court in an action filed by the donor against the donee, so the donor cannot revoke by a unilateral act of his own.
The court cannot entertain the revocation action unless it is filed both within ten years of the execution of the deed of gift and within two years of the date on which the cause of action arose.

An application for registration of the action as a lis pendens must be filed in court with the plaint, addressed to the Registrar of Lands of the district in which the deed is registered or, if it is unregistered, of the district in which the land lies.
A duly registered lis pendens is deemed pending from the time of registration even before summons is served, which is why registration protects the donor while the action is on foot.
The revocation action is proceeded with and regulated by the procedure of the Civil Procedure Code.
Because the donee refuses to join in a cancellation, no consensual undoing of the deed is available and the donor must proceed by the statutory action against the donee.

The donee's alleged conduct, withholding food and medicine from the elderly donor, assaulting him and evicting him from the gifted house, is the conduct relied on as gross ingratitude, and whether it meets that standard is for the court because the Act supplies no definition.

An action filed in or about October 2019 is roughly one year and seven months after the deed was executed on 12 March 2018 and about five months after the cause of action arose on 20 May 2019, so both limbs of the time bar are satisfied.
Since the deed is registered in the Gampaha land registry, the lis pendens application filed with the plaint is addressed to the Registrar of Lands of the Gampaha district.

The deed can be revoked despite stating that it is absolute and irrevocable, but only by an order of a competent court on the ground of gross ingratitude in an action by the donor against the donee, filed within both limbs of the time bar, accompanied by a lis pendens application and prosecuted under the Civil Procedure Code.
The donor cannot obtain revocation merely by asserting the ground; the outcome depends on the court being satisfied on the evidence that the donee's proved conduct amounts to gross ingratitude.

enrichment.original_background: A Deed of Gift States that it is absolute and irrevocable.
enrichment.enriched_background: By a Deed of Gift bearing No. 2418 dated 12 March 2018, attested by a notary public at Kadawatha, Wimalasena Perera, a retired schoolmaster of Kadawatha, gifted to his nephew Chandana Perera the land and two-storeyed dwelling house called Sirisara Watta, eighteen perches in extent, situated at Kadawatha in the District of Gampaha. The deed was registered in the Gampaha land registry on 3 April 2018. The deed states that it is absolute and irrevocable, and no life interest, fiduciary interest or right of residence was reserved in it. After the gift Wimalasena, who is now seventy-four, continued to live in the house with his nephew's agreement. From February 2019 Chandana stopped supplying the donor with food and medicine, and in the course of a quarrel over the property he assaulted him. On 20 May 2019 he locked the donor out of the house and had the donor's belongings removed to a relative's home, where the donor has lived since. In October 2019 Wimalasena instructs an attorney-at-law that he wishes to have the gift undone. Chandana refuses to join in any cancellation of the deed and denies that he has done anything wrong.

added_facts.fact: The donor is Wimalasena Perera, a retired schoolmaster of Kadawatha; the donee is his nephew Chandana Perera.
added_facts.reason: The question as set names no parties. Section 2 frames the remedy as an action by the donor against the donee, so the scenario needs identified parties in those two roles.
added_facts.counterfactual_effect: Neutral as to outcome. If the person seeking revocation were someone other than the donor, an heir for example, section 2 would not give that person the action.

added_facts.fact: The subject matter is the land and two-storeyed dwelling house called Sirisara Watta, eighteen perches in extent, at Kadawatha in the District of Gampaha.
added_facts.reason: The question does not say what was gifted. Immovable property in an identified district is needed because the lis pendens application is district-specific.
added_facts.counterfactual_effect: Neutral as to whether the gift can be revoked. It fixes Gampaha as the district for the lis pendens application; a different district would only change the addressee.

added_facts.fact: The deed bears No. 2418, was executed on 12 March 2018 before a notary public, and was registered in the Gampaha land registry on 3 April 2018.
added_facts.reason: The ten-year limb of the time bar runs from the date of execution, and the addressee of the lis pendens application depends on whether the deed is registered. Neither can be applied without an execution date and a registration status.
added_facts.counterfactual_effect: Decisive. An execution date more than ten years before filing would bar the action outright. An execution date before the 2017 Act would raise a question the corpus cannot answer. If the deed were unregistered, the lis pendens application would go to the Registrar of the district where the land lies rather than the district of registration.

added_facts.fact: From February 2019 the donee stopped supplying the elderly donor with food and medicine, assaulted him during a quarrel over the property, and on 20 May 2019 locked him out of the gifted house and had his belongings removed.
added_facts.reason: Section 2 allows revocation on one ground only. Without pleaded conduct on the donee's part there is nothing capable of amounting to gross ingratitude and the question has no determinate answer.
added_facts.counterfactual_effect: Decisive. If the donee had done nothing of this kind, no ground under section 2 would exist and the deed could not be revoked at all. Whether this particular conduct is held to be gross ingratitude remains for the court, since the Act does not define the term.

added_facts.fact: The eviction on 20 May 2019 is the latest act complained of, the donor instructs an attorney-at-law in October 2019, and the donee refuses to join in any cancellation of the deed.
added_facts.reason: The second limb of section 3 runs two years from the date the cause of action arose, so the scenario needs a date for that. The donee's refusal removes any consensual cancellation and leaves the statutory action as the only route.
added_facts.counterfactual_effect: Decisive. If the last act complained of were more than two years before filing, the court could not entertain the action even though the ten-year limb was satisfied. If the donee agreed to a cancellation, the parties could deal with the matter by a further notarial instrument and no court order would be needed.

legal_issues.issue: Whether a Deed of Gift of land and a house in Kohuwala falls within the Western Provincial Council's stamp duty charge, so that a Provincial Assessor of Revenue values it.
What 'value' the Assessor must ascertain for gifted immovable property, and which limb of the statutory definition applies where the donor acquired the property in March 1978.
How the cost of the house built after acquisition and the present market value of the whole property enter that computation.

gold_answer_draft.issue: How a Provincial Assessor of Revenue attached to the Western Provincial Council arrives at the value of the Kohuwala land and house for stamp duty purposes on the proposed Deed of Gift from Nimal Perera to his son Aruna.
gold_answer_draft.rule: Stamp duty is charged on every instrument relating to a transfer of immovable property situated in the Western Province (Western Province Financial Statute No. 6 of 1990, s.37(a)), and 'Transfer' is defined in s.106 to include a gift, so a Deed of Gift is chargeable. By s.48(1) the duty is calculated on the 'value' of the property conveyed. 'Value' is defined in s.106. Because a 'gift' is a transfer made voluntarily and without consideration in money or money's worth, the gift limbs of that definition apply rather than the ordinary open-market limb. Where the gifted immovable property was acquired by the donor after 31 March 1977, paragraph (c) of the definition of 'value' requires the Assessor to compare two figures: (i) the price which in his opinion the property would have fetched if sold in the open market on the date the donor acquired it, increased by the cost of improvements, alterations and additions made after acquisition and before the date of the deed of gift; and (ii) the price which in his opinion the property would have fetched if sold in the open market on the date of the instrument of gift. The value is whichever of the two is lower. Both figures are the Assessor's own opinion, and for that purpose s.63 lets him call for any document or other evidence needed to prove the facts bearing on chargeability and amount, on an adjudication under s.62 which ends in a written determination and an endorsement under s.64.
gold_answer_draft.application: Nimal Perera acquired the 26-perch Kohuwala land in March 1978, which is after 31 March 1977, so paragraph (c) of the definition of 'value' governs and paragraph (b), which uses a 31 March 1977 base, does not. For limb (i) the Assessor forms an opinion of the open-market price of the property on the date of acquisition in March 1978; the Rs.120,000 paid on the 1978 purchase is the evidence of that price, although the test is the Assessor's opinion of the open-market price and not the recited consideration. To that he adds the cost of the improvements made after acquisition and before the deed of gift, namely the Rs.2,900,000 spent on constructing the house, giving Rs.120,000 + Rs.2,900,000 = Rs.3,020,000. For limb (ii) the Assessor forms an opinion of what the land and house together would fetch in the open market on the date of the Deed of Gift, which on the instructions is Rs.5,700,000. He then takes the lower of the two, and Rs.3,020,000 is lower than Rs.5,700,000. In arriving at each figure the Assessor may under s.63 require production of the 1978 deed of purchase, the building plan and the bills, receipts or a quantity surveyor's statement evidencing the Rs.2,900,000 construction cost, and material on current prices in Kohuwala; he is not bound by the parties' own figures, so both limbs remain open until he is satisfied on the evidence. The notary drawing the deed must independently satisfy himself under s.78(2) that the value on which duty is paid represents the value of the property conveyed.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: The Assessor does not simply take the present market value of Rs.5,700,000. Applying paragraph (c) of the definition of 'value' in s.106 of the Western Province Financial Statute No. 6 of 1990, he compares the March 1978 open-market price of Rs.120,000 increased by the Rs.2,900,000 cost of constructing the house, that is Rs.3,020,000, with the open-market price at the date of the gift of Rs.5,700,000, and adopts the lower figure. The value of the property for stamp duty on this Deed of Gift is therefore Rs.3,020,000, subject to the Assessor's own opinion of the two open-market prices on the evidence produced to him.

answer_claims.claim_text: Stamp duty is charged on every instrument relating to a transfer of immovable property situated in the Western Province, at the prescribed rate.
A Deed of Gift falls within that charge because 'Transfer' is defined to include a gift.
The duty is calculated on the value of the property conveyed, not on the consideration recited in the instrument.
A gift is a transfer made voluntarily and without consideration in money or money's worth, so the gift limbs of the definition of 'value' apply.

For gifted immovable property acquired by the donor after 31 March 1977, 'value' is the lower of (i) the Assessor's opinion of the open-market price on the date of acquisition increased by the cost of post-acquisition improvements made before the deed of gift, and (ii) his opinion of the open-market price on the date of the instrument of gift.

Both figures are the opinion of a Provincial Assessor of Revenue appointed under the Statute, and on an adjudication he may require production of documents or other evidence to prove the facts bearing on chargeability and amount.
Because Nimal Perera acquired the Kohuwala land in March 1978, which is after 31 March 1977, paragraph (c) of the definition of 'value' applies and not the 31 March 1977 base in paragraph (b).

Under limb (i) the Assessor takes the open-market price at acquisition in March 1978, evidenced by the Rs.120,000 purchase price, and adds the Rs.2,900,000 cost of constructing the house after acquisition, giving Rs.3,020,000.
Under limb (ii) the Assessor takes the open-market price of the land and house at the date of the Deed of Gift, which on the instructions is Rs.5,700,000.
The Assessor may call for the 1978 deed of purchase and the bills or receipts evidencing the construction cost before accepting either figure, and is not bound by the parties' own valuation.
The value of the property for stamp duty on this Deed of Gift is Rs.3,020,000, being the lower of Rs.3,020,000 and Rs.5,700,000, and not the present market value of Rs.5,700,000.

enrichment.original_background: In 1978 March Nimal Perera had purchased a land in extent of 26 Perches situated in Kohuwala for Rs.120,000/- and constructed a house on it. The cost of construction of the house was Rs. 2,900,000/- He wishes to gift this house and land to his son Aruna and instructs you to prepare a Deed of Gift. The present market value of the house and property is Rs.5,700,000/-
